At last, however, on the eve of All Saints’, as Fra Serafino tells us, Carmagnola accompanied by Valeria and her brother bore word himself to Bellarion that the bridges were ready and that a party of fifty of his men were encamped on the peninsula between the rivers. He came to demand that Bellarion should so dispose that the army should begin to cross at dawn.

“That,” said Bellarion, “assumes that your bridges endure until dawn.”

He was standing, where he had risen to receive his visitors, in the middle of his roomy pavilion, which was lighted by a group of three lanterns hung at the height of his head on the tent-pole. The book in which he had been reading was closed upon his forefinger.

“Endure until dawn?” Carmagnola was annoyed by the suggestion. “What do you mean?”

Bellarion’s remark had been imprudent. Still more imprudent was the laugh he now uttered.

===Chinese===
这几座桥并没有像预言的那样一周完工，而是足足花了十一天的工夫。然而，正如塞拉菲诺修士（Fra Serafino）所记述的那样，在诸圣节前夜，卡尔马尼奥拉在瓦莱里娅与她弟弟的陪同下，亲自前来向贝拉里翁报信，称桥梁已全部架设妥当，他已派出一支五十人的分队驻扎在两河之间的半岛上，特来要求贝拉里翁即刻部署，让大军于拂晓时分开始渡河。

“那得有一个前提，”贝拉里翁说道，“就是你的桥能撑到天亮。”

他刚才起身迎接访客，此刻正站在宽敞的大帐中央。帐篷中柱与他齐头高的地方悬着一簇三盏灯笼，照亮了四周。他手里那本刚才正在读的书已然合上，食指夹在书页之间。

“撑到天亮？”卡尔马尼奥拉被他这话激怒了，“你这话是什么意思？”

贝拉里翁那句话本已失之轻率；而他此刻发出的那声冷笑，更是愈发轻率。

===Original===
“Ask yourself who should destroy them,” he said. “In your place I should have asked myself that before I went to the trouble of building them.”

“How should Theodore know of it, shut up as he is in Vercelli, eight miles away?”

Part of his question was answered on the instant by a demoniac uproar from the strip of land across the water. Cries of rage and terror, shouts of encouragement and command, the sound of blows, and all the unmistakable din of conflict, rose fiercely upon the deepening gloom.

“He knows, it seems,” said Bellarion, and again he laughed.

===Chinese===
“你不妨问问自己，会是谁来毁掉它们，”他说道，“换作是我，在费心费力去造这些桥之前，早就先问过自己这个问题了。”

“西奥多被困在八英里外的韦尔切利，他怎么可能知道这事？”

他话音刚落，对岸那片狭长的河洲上便骤然爆发出鬼哭狼嚎般的喧嚣，顷刻间便替他回答了一半的疑问。愤怒与惊恐的喊叫、鼓舞与号令的嘶吼、兵刃交击的碰撞声，以及一切不容错辨的厮杀喧阗，在愈渐浓重的夜色中猛烈地腾起。

“看来他已经知道了。”贝拉里翁说着，又冷笑了一声。

===Original===
Carmagnola stood a moment, clenching and unclenching his hands, his face white with rage. Then he span round where he stood and with an inarticulate cry dashed from the tent.

One withering glance Valeria flashed into Bellarion’s sardonically amused countenance, then, summoning her brother, she followed Carmagnola.

Bellarion set down his book upon the table by the tent-pole, took up a cloak, and followed them at leisure, through the screen of bare trees behind which his pavilion had been pitched, and along the high bank of the swirling river towards the head of Carmagnola’s bridge.

There, as he expected, he found them, scarcely visible in the gloom, and with them a knot of men-at-arms and a half-dozen stragglers, all that had escaped of the party that Carmagnola had sent across an hour ago. The others had been surrounded and captured. Last of all to win across, arriving just as Bellarion reached the spot, was Belluno, who had commanded them, an excitable Neapolitan who leapt up the bank from the bridge ranting by all the patrons of Naples that they had been betrayed.

===Chinese===
卡尔马尼奥拉僵立片刻，双拳紧握又松开，松开又握紧，气得脸色铁青。随即他猛一转身，发出一声含混不清的怒吼，冲出了大帐。

瓦莱里娅向贝拉里翁那张带着讥诮笑意的脸庞投去凌厉冰冷的一瞥，旋即唤上弟弟，紧随卡尔马尼奥拉追了出去。

贝拉里翁将书放到帐柱旁的桌案上，披上一件斗篷，不慌不忙地跟在他们后面，穿过那片光秃秃的林木掩体——他的营帐就扎在这片树林后——沿着汹涌奔流的河岸高堤，朝卡尔马尼奥拉所建的桥头走去。

果不出他所料，他在那里找到了他们。众人的身影在昏暗的夜色中几不可辨，身旁还簇拥着一小队重甲兵和五六个逃回来的散兵游勇——这便是卡尔马尼奥拉一小时前派过河去的那支分队中仅存的逃生者了。其余的人悉数被围困擒获。最后一个奋力逃过桥来的，正是率领这支分队的指挥官贝卢诺，他恰在贝拉里翁赶到现场的那一刻抵岸。这位性情急躁的那不勒斯人（Neapolitan）从桥上纵身跃上河堤，指着那不勒斯（Naples）所有的守护圣徒破口大骂，声称他们遭人出卖了。

===Original===
Over the river came a sound of tramping feet. Dimly reflected in the water they could see the forms of men who otherwise moved invisible on the farther bank, and presently came a sound of axes on timber.

“There goes your bridge, Francesco,” said Bellarion, and for the third time he laughed.

“Do you mock me, damn you!” Carmagnola raged at him, and then raised his voice to roar for arbalesters. Three or four of the men went off vociferously, at a run, to fetch them, whilst Valeria turned suddenly upon Bellarion, whose tall cloaked figure stood beside her.

“Why do you laugh?” Her voice, sharp with disdain, resentment, and suspicion, silenced all there that they might hear his answer.

“I am human, I suppose, and, therefore, not entirely without malice.”

===Chinese===
河对岸传来杂沓的脚步声。对岸黑漆漆的，原本看不见人影，可水面上隐约映出些晃动的轮廓；紧接着，便传来了利斧劈砍木料的声响。

“你的桥完蛋了，弗朗切斯科，”贝拉里翁说道，随即第三次笑出了声。

“该死的，你竟敢嘲笑我！”卡尔马尼奥拉冲他咆哮起来，随后提高嗓门大吼着传唤弩手。三四个士兵连声应喝着飞奔去调人，瓦莱里娅则猛地转过身，直视着身旁那道披着斗篷的高大身影。

“你笑什么？”她的声音因鄙夷、愤恨与猜疑而尖利刺耳，在场众人顿时鸦雀无声，齐齐等着听他的回答。

“大概因为我也是个凡人，所以难免也带点恶意吧。”

===Original===
“Is that all your reason? Is your malice so deep that you can laugh at an enemy advantage which may wreck the labour of days?” And then with increasing sharpness and increasing accusation: “You knew!” she cried. “You knew that the bridges would be destroyed tonight. Yourself, you said so. How did you know? How did you know?”

“What are you implying, madonna?” cried Carmagnola, aghast. For all his hostility towards Bellarion, he was very far from ready to believe that he played a double game.

“That I have no wits,” said Bellarion, quietly scornful.

And now the impetuous Belluno, smarting under his own particular misadventure and near escape, must needs cut in.

“Madonna is implying more than that. She is implying that you’ve sold us to Theodore of Montferrat.”

===Chinese===
“这就是你的全部理由？你的恶意竟深重到这种地步，连敌人占了上风、险些毁掉数日心血，你都能笑得出来？”紧接着，她的语气愈发严厉，指控之意也越来越浓：“你早知道！”她喝道，“你早知道这几座桥今晚会被毁掉！是你自己亲口这么说的！你怎么会知道的？你怎么会知道！”

“夫人，您这是什么意思？”卡尔马尼奥拉大惊失色地叫道。尽管他对贝拉里翁满怀敌意，却远未做好准备相信对方竟会暗中通敌、玩弄两面派。

“她在说我蠢笨无能罢了。”贝拉里翁平静地说道，语带轻蔑。

这时，性情鲁莽的贝卢诺刚经历了一番狼狈溃逃，死里逃生正窝着一肚子火，偏要抢上前插上一嘴。

“夫人暗指的可不止这个。她是在说，你把我们卖给蒙费拉托的西奥多了！”

===Original===
“Are you implying it, too, Belluno?” His tone had changed. There was now in his voice a note that the Princess had never heard, a note that made Belluno’s blood run cold. “Speak out, man! Though I give licence for innuendo to a lady, I require clear speech from every man. So let us have this thing quite plainly.”

Belluno was brave and obstinate. He conquered his fear of Bellarion sufficiently to make a show of standing his ground.

“It is clear,” he answered sullenly, “that we have been betrayed.”

“How is it clear, you fool?” Bellarion shifted again from cold wrath with an insubordinate inferior to argument with a fellow man. “Are you so inept at the trade by which you live that you can conceive of a soldier in the Marquis Theodore’s position neglecting to throw out scouts to watch the enemy and report his movements? Are you so much a fool as that? If so, I shall have to think of replacing you in your command.”

Carmagnola interposed aggressively; and this partly to protect Belluno who was one of his own lieutenants, and partly because the sneer at the fellow’s lack of military foresight was a reflection upon Carmagnola himself.

===Chinese===
“贝卢诺，难道你也是这个意思？”贝拉里翁的语气骤然一变。此刻他声音里透出的那股寒意，是公主从未听过的，听得贝卢诺浑身血液都要冻僵了。“有话直说，汉子！一位贵妇人含沙射影，我可以容忍；但凡是个男人，在我面前就得把话敞亮着说出来。来吧，咱们把事情摆到明面上讲个清楚。”

贝卢诺既勇敢又固执。他勉强压下对贝拉里翁的畏惧，硬着头皮摆出一副寸步不让的架势。

“明摆着的事，”他沉着脸答道，“我们被人出卖了。”

“怎么就明摆着了，你这蠢货？”贝拉里翁又从对犯上作乱的下属的森然震怒，转回到了与常人讲道理的口吻。“难道你对自己赖以为生的行当竟一窍不通到这种地步，连身处西奥多侯爵（Marquis Theodore）那般境地的统帅，会疏忽到不派出斥候监视敌情、探报敌军动向这种事都信得出来？你真蠢到那个地步了吗？若真是如此，我可就得考虑撤掉你的兵权、另择贤能了。”

卡尔马尼奥拉气势汹汹地横插进来——此举一来是为了袒护自己麾下的爱将贝卢诺，二来是因为嘲讽这名部将缺乏军事远见，无异于指着卡尔马尼奥拉自己的鼻子骂他无能。

===Original===
“Do you pretend that you foresaw this action of Theodore’s?”

“I pretend that any but a fool must have foreseen it. It is precisely what any soldier in his place would do: allow you to waste time, material, and energy on building bridges, and then promptly destroy them for you.”

“Why, then, did you not say this ten days ago?”

“Why?” Bellarion’s voice sounded amused. His face they could not see. “Because I never spend myself in argument with those who learn only by experience.”

Again the Princess intervened. “Is that the best reason you can give? You allowed time, material, and energy, and now even a detachment of men to be wasted, merely that you might prove his folly to my Lord of Carmagnola? Is that what you ask us to believe?”

===Chinese===
“照你这么说，你是早就料到西奥多会来这一手了？”

“我敢说，只要不是蠢货，任谁都料得到。换作任何一名将领处在他的位置上，都会这么干：先放任你把时间、木料和人力白白耗在架桥上，等桥一搭好，再干脆利落地替你毁掉。”

“那十天前你为什么不这么说？”

“为什么？”贝拉里翁的声音听起来兴味盎然，只是夜色下众人看不清他的面容，“因为对于那些只有亲身碰壁才肯长记性的人，我从不费唇舌去争辩。”

公主再次开口质问：“这就是你能给出的最好解释吗？你坐视宝贵的时间、物资与人力白白浪费，甚至连一支分队的弟兄都折损了，仅仅是为了向卡尔马尼奥拉大人证明他的愚蠢？你就要我们相信这样的鬼话吗？”

===Original===
“He thinks us credulous, by God!” swore Carmagnola.

Bellarion kept his patience. “I had another reason, a military one with which it seems that I must shame your wits. To move the whole army from here to Carpignano would have taken me at least two days, perhaps three. A mounted detachment from Vercelli to destroy the bridge could reach Carpignano in a few hours, and once it was seen that I moved my army thither that detachment would have been instantly despatched. It was a movement I feared in any case, until your bridge-building operations here deceived Theodore into believing that I had no thought of Carpignano. That is why I allowed them to continue. Though your bridges could never serve the purpose for which you built them, they could excellently serve to disguise my own intention of crossing at Carpignano. Tomorrow, when the army begins to move thither, that detachment of Theodore’s will most certainly be sent to destroy the bridge. But it will find it held by a thousand men under Stoffel, and the probable capture of that detachment will compensate for the loss of men you have suffered tonight.”

There was a moment’s utter silence when he had done, a silence of defeat and confusion. Then came an applauding splutter of laughter from the group of men and officers who stood about.

It was cut short by a loud crash from across the stream, and, thereafter, with a groaning and rending of timbers, a gurgling of swelling, momentarily arrested, waters, and finally a noise like a thunderclap, the wrecked bridge swinging out into the stream snapped from the logs that held it to the northern shore.

===Chinese===
“上帝作证，他把我们当成傻子骗呢！”卡尔马尼奥拉咒骂道。

贝拉里翁按捺住性子：“我还有另一个原因——一个军事上的考量，看来我非得拿出来羞辱一番你们的才智不可。把全军从这里调往卡尔皮尼亚诺，至少需要两天，或许三天；而从韦尔切利派出一支骑兵分队去炸毁那座桥，只需几个小时就能赶到。一旦敌军察觉我军向那儿移动，那支骑兵必然立刻出动。这原本是我无论如何都要提防的一步棋——直到你在这里大张旗鼓地架桥，把西奥多骗得团团转，让他以为我根本没打算走卡尔皮尼亚诺。正因如此，我才放任你们继续施工。你的桥虽说绝不可能派上你原本指望的用场，却恰恰绝妙地掩盖了我打算从卡尔皮尼亚诺渡河的真正意图。明天一早，等大军开始往那儿开拔，西奥多那支骑兵分队必定会被派去拆桥。可等他们赶到那儿，就会发现桥头正由斯托费尔麾下一千名精兵把守；把那支骑兵分队一举擒获，足以抵消你今晚折损的这批人手。”

他话音落地，四周陷入了片刻死一般的寂静——那是挫败与错愕交织的沉默。紧接着，围站在旁边的士兵与军官们中间，爆发出了一阵喝彩般的哄笑。

笑声随即被河对岸传来的一声巨响打断。紧接着，伴随着木梁痛苦的呻吟与撕裂声、暴涨的河水短暂受阻后发出的咕噜翻涌声，以及最后如同霹雳炸响般的轰鸣，那座被毁坏的桥梁顺着水流猛地甩向河心，从固定在北岸的圆木上彻底折断。

===Original===
“There it goes, Carmagnola,” said Bellarion. “But you no longer need bewail your labours. They have served my purpose.”

He cast his cloak more tightly about him, wished them good night almost gaily, and went striding away towards his pavilion.

Carmagnola, crestfallen, swallowing his chagrin as best he could, stood there in silence beside the equally silenced Princess.

Belluno swore softly, and vented a laugh of some little bitterness.

“He’s deep, always deep, by Saint Januarius! Never does he do the things he seems to do. Never does he aim where he looks.”

===Chinese===
“它顺水漂走了，卡尔马尼奥拉，”贝拉里翁说道，“不过你再也不必哀叹自己白费心血了。你的桥，已经替我派上了用场。”

他把斗篷往身上裹紧了些，几乎是欢快地向众人道了声晚安，便迈开大步朝自己的大帐走去。

卡尔马尼奥拉垂头丧气，强自咽下满腹懊恼，一言不发地矗立在同样沉默不语的公主身旁。

贝卢诺低声咒骂了一句，发出一声带着几分苦涩的冷笑。

“圣雅努阿里乌斯（Saint Januarius）在上，他城府太深了，向来深不可测！他做的事，从来不是表面上看起来那样；他瞄准的地方，也从来不是他眼睛望过去的方向。”

## IX Vercelli / 第九章 韦尔切利

===Original===
A letter survives which the Prince of Valsassina wrote some little time after these events to Duke Filippo Maria, in which occurs the following criticism of the captains of his day: “They are stout fellows and great fighters, but rude, unlettered, and lacking culture. Their minds are fertile, vigorous soil, but unbroken by the plough of learning, so that the seeds of knowledge with which they are all too sparsely sown find little root there.”

At Carpignano, when they came there three days after breaking camp, they found that all had fallen out as Bellarion calculated. A detachment of horse one hundred strong had been sent in haste with the necessary implements to destroy the bridge. That detachment Stoffel had surrounded, captured, disarmed, and disbanded.

They crossed, and after another three days marching down the right bank of the Sesia they crossed the Cervo just above Quinto, where Bellarion took up his quarters in the little castle owned there by the Lord Girolamo Prato, who was with Theodore in Vercelli.

Here, too, were housed the Princess and her brother and the Lord of Carmagnola, the latter by now recovered from his humiliation in the matter of his bridges to a state of normal self-complacency and arrogance.

===Chinese===
瓦尔萨西纳亲王在这些事发生后不久，曾给菲利波·玛丽亚公爵写过一封信，信件至今尚存，其中对当世将领有这样一番评述：“他们个个勇武善战，却粗鄙不文、腹中空空。他们的头脑原是肥沃而有生气的良田，只可惜未经学问之犁翻耕，以致那稀稀落落撒进去的几粒知识种子，也难在里头生根发芽。”

拔营三日后，大军行至卡尔皮尼亚诺，果见一切皆如贝拉里翁所料。敌方此前仓促派出一支百人骑兵分队，携带着拆桥器具前来毁桥，已被斯托费尔团团围住、尽数俘获，缴械后就地遣散。

大军顺利渡河，沿着塞西亚河右岸又行军三日，在昆托上游不远处渡过切尔沃河（Cervo）。贝拉里翁便在昆托落脚，住进了吉罗拉莫·普拉托勋爵（Girolamo Prato）的那座小城堡——而这位普拉托勋爵眼下正随西奥多守在韦尔切利城内。

公主与她弟弟，以及卡尔马尼奥拉勋爵也都安顿在此处。那位卡尔马尼奥拉历经浮桥受挫的羞辱后，如今已然缓过劲来，又恢复了往日那副自鸣得意、目中无人的常态。

===Original===
An eighteenth-century French writer on tactics, M. Dévinequi, in his *L’Art Militaire au Moyen Age*, in the course of a lengthy comparison between the methods of Bellarion Cane and the almost equally famous Sir John Hawkwood, offers some strong adverse criticisms upon Bellarion’s dispositions in the case of this siege of Vercelli. He considers that as a necessary measure of preparation Bellarion when at Quinto should have thrown bridges across the Sesia above and below the city, so as to maintain unbroken his lines of circumvallation, instead of contenting himself with ferrying a force across to guard the eastern approaches. This force, being cut off by the river, could, says M. Dévinequi, neither be supported at need nor afford support.

What the distinguished French writer has missed is the fact that, once engaged upon it, Bellarion was as little in earnest about the siege of Vercelli as he was about Carmagnola’s bridges. The one as much as the other was no more than a strategic demonstration. From the outset﻿—that is to say, from the time when arriving at Quinto he beheld the strong earthworks Theodore had thrown up﻿—he realised that the place was not easily to be carried by assault, and it was within his knowledge that it was too well victualled to succumb to hunger save after a siege more protracted than he himself was prepared to impose upon it.

===Chinese===
十八世纪有位研究兵法的法国著作家德维内基先生（M. Dévinequi），在其著作《中世纪军事艺术》（*L’Art Militaire au Moyen Age*）中，曾用长篇大论将贝拉里翁·卡内与名声几乎不相上下的约翰·霍克伍德爵士（Sir John Hawkwood）的战法逐一比对，其间对贝拉里翁在此次韦尔切利围城战中的兵力部署提出了严厉批评。他认为，贝拉里翁驻军昆托时，本应事先在城池上下游各架一座浮桥横跨塞西亚河，以维持围城战线首尾相连，而不该仅满足于摆渡一支部队过河去扼守东面通道。德维内基先生指出，那支部队被大河隔断，战事吃紧时既得不到本阵驰援，也无法去接应本阵。

这位杰出的法国著作家有所不知的是：自打这场战事打响，贝拉里翁对围攻韦尔切利一事的敷衍，就跟对卡尔马尼奥拉的浮桥一般无二。前者与后者一样，统统不过是场虚张声势的战略佯动。打从一开始——确切地说，打从他抵达昆托、望见西奥多构筑的那一道道坚固土垒起——他便心里有数：此城绝非强攻所能轻易拿下；况且他也早探明城中粮草充足，除非长期死困，否则断不会因饥馑而降，而他自己并不打算耗上那么长久的时日。

===Original===
But there was Carmagnola, swaggering and thrasonical in spite of all that had gone, and there was the Princess Valeria supporting the handsome condottiero with her confidence. And Carmagnola, not content that Bellarion should girdle the city, arguing reasonably enough that months would be entailed in bringing Theodore to surrender from hunger, was loud and insistent in his demands that the place be assaulted. Once again, as in the case of the bridges, Bellarion yielded to the other’s overbearing insistence, went even the length of inviting him to plan and conduct the assaults. Three of these were delivered, and all three repulsed with ease by an enemy that appeared to Bellarion to be uncannily prescient. After the third repulse, the same suspicion occurred to Carmagnola, and he expressed it; not, however, to Bellarion, as he should have done, but to the Princess.

“You mean,” she said, “that someone on our side is conveying information to Theodore of our intentions?”

They were alone together in the armoury of the Castle of Quinto whose pointed windows overlooked the river. It was normally a bare room with stone walls and a vaulted white ceiling up which crawled a troop of the rampant lions of the Prati crudely frescoed in a dingy red. Bellarion had brought to it some furnishings that made it habitable, and so it became the room they chiefly used.

===Chinese===
然而军中偏有个卡尔马尼奥拉，尽管吃过前番的亏，依旧大摇大摆、不可一世；更有瓦莱里娅公主在一旁对这位相貌堂堂的雇佣兵统帅偏信有加。卡尔马尼奥拉不满贝拉里翁只围不攻，振振有词地辩称单靠饿死西奥多非得拖上几个月不可，因此大声疾呼、执意要求强攻城池。一如先前造桥之事，贝拉里翁再度向对方的嚣张固执让步，甚至索性请他亲自筹划并指挥攻城。三轮强攻接连发动，结果三战皆墨，被守军轻而易举地击退——在贝拉里翁看来，敌军简直像未卜先知一般诡异。第三次败退下来后，卡尔马尼奥拉也生出了同样的疑心，并且吐露了出来；只是他没按规矩向贝拉里翁禀报，反倒跑去跟公主说了。

“你的意思是，”她问道，“我们这边有人暗中把我们的动向透漏给了西奥多？”

此刻二人正独处在昆托城堡的军械室里，尖拱窗外俯瞰着滔滔河水。这屋子平日里四壁石墙空荡荡的，白灰拱顶上用暗淡的红颜料粗劣地画着一队张牙舞爪的普拉托家族（Prati）雄狮，一路攀援而上。贝拉里翁让人搬来几件家具陈设，才使它勉强能住人，于是这里便成了他们最常议事的地方。

===Original===
The Princess sat by the table in a great chair of painted leather, faded but comfortable. She was wrapped in a long blue gown that was lined with lynx fur against the chill weather which had set in. Carmagnola, big and gaudy in a suit of the colour of sulphur, his tunic reversed with black fur, his powerful yet shapely legs booted to the knee, strode to and fro across the room in his excitement.

“It is what I begin to fear,” he answered her, and resumed his pacing.

A silence followed, and remained unbroken until he went to plant himself, his feet wide, his hands behind him, before the logs that blazed in the cavernous fireplace.

She looked up and met his glance. “You know what I am thinking,” he said. “I am wondering whether you may not be right, after all, in your suspicions.”

Gently she shook her head. “I dismissed them on that night when your bridges were destroyed. His vindication was so complete, what followed proved him so right, that I could suspect him no longer. He is just a mercenary fellow, fighting for the hand that pays. I trust him now because he must know that he can win more by loyalty than by treachery.”

===Chinese===
公主坐在桌旁一张宽大的彩绘皮椅上，椅面虽已褪色却甚是舒适。天已转凉，她裹着一件镶着猞猁毛皮衬里的蓝色长袍。卡尔马尼奥拉则身穿一袭扎眼的硫磺色衣裤，外袍翻出黑毛皮里子，一双粗壮却不失匀称的小腿蹬着齐膝长靴，在屋里兴奋地踱来踱去，显得人高马大又花哨。

“眼下我正是担心这个。”他答了一句，又继续来回踱步。

屋里安静下来，直到他走到那座洞穴般深阔的壁炉前，劈开双脚站定，双手背在身后，面前原木正熊熊燃烧。

她抬起眼，迎上他的目光。“你晓得我在想什么，”他开口道，“我在琢磨，说到底，先前你的疑心怕不是真有道理。”

她轻轻摇了摇头。“你那几座浮桥被毁的那天夜里，我就打消这个念头了。他把话说得那样透彻，后来的战局又证明他算得那样准，我实在没法再怀疑他。他不过是个拿钱卖命的雇佣兵罢了，谁给钱就替谁打仗。我如今信他，是因为他自己心里必定明白，忠心效力比背主求荣捞到的好处多得多。”

===Original===
“Aye,” he agreed, “you are right, my Princess. You are always right.”

“I was not right in my suspicions of him. So think no more of those.”

Standing as he did, he was completely screening the fire from her. She rose and crossed to it, holding out her hands to the blaze when he made room for her beside him.

“I am chilled,” she said. “As much, I think, by our want of progress as by these November winds.”

“Nay, but take heart, Valeria,” he bade her. “The one will last no longer than the other. Spring will follow in the world and in your soul.”

She looked up at him, and found him good to look upon, so big and strong, so handsome and so confident.

“It is heartening to have such a man as you for company in such days.”

He took her in his arms, a masterful, irresistible fellow.

“With such a woman as you beside me, Valeria, I could conquer the world.”

===Chinese===
“嗯，”他连声附和，“你说得对，我的公主。你总是对的。”

“我先前怀疑他，可就不对。别再往那上头想了。”

他这么往炉前一站，把火光严严实实挡了个全。她起身走过去，待他在身旁让出空当，便伸出双手去烤那团旺火。

“我身上冷得很，”她说，“想来一半是因为这十一月的寒风，一半也是因为战事迟迟不见寸进。”

“别灰心，瓦莱里娅，”他安慰道，“这僵局不会比这阵寒风更长久。春天总会降临人间，也会降临你的心头。”

她仰起脸望向他，只觉他生得实在好看——那样魁梧强壮，那样英俊潇洒，又那样意气风发。

“在这等煎熬的日子里，有你这样的男子相伴，真教人心里踏实。”

他一把将她揽入怀中，浑身透着一股霸道而教人难以抗拒的男子气概。

“瓦莱里娅，有你这样的女子陪在身旁，我连天下都能征服。”

===Original===
A dry voice broke in upon that rapture: “You might make a beginning by conquering Vercelli.”

Starting guiltily apart, they met the mocking eyes of Bellarion who entered. He came forward easily, as handsome in his way as Carmagnola, but cast in a finer, statelier mould. “I should be grateful to you, Francesco, and so would her highness, if you would accomplish that. The world can wait until afterwards.”

And Carmagnola, to cover his confusion and Valeria’s, plunged headlong into contention.

“I’d reduce Vercelli tomorrow if I had my way.”

“Who hinders you?”

“You do. There was that night attack﻿ ﻿…”

“Oh, that!” said Bellarion. “Do you bring that up again? Will you never take my word for anything, I wonder? It is foredoomed to failure.”

===Chinese===
一声冷冰冰的嗓音骤然打断了这份沉醉：“你不妨先从征服韦尔切利下手。”

二人做贼心虚般猛地弹开，正撞上推门进来的贝拉里翁那双满含戏谑的眼睛。他从容不迫地走上前，论相貌自有一番不输卡尔马尼奥拉的俊朗，只是骨子里更显清贵高华。“弗朗切斯科，你若能把这城拿下来，我感激不尽，殿下也感激不尽。至于征服天下，大可以往后放一放。”

卡尔马尼奥拉为了掩饰自己与瓦莱里娅的窘迫，一头扎进争辩里。

“若依着我的法子来，明日我就能拿下韦尔切利。”

“谁拦着你了？”

“就是你。先前我提议的那场夜袭……”

“哦，那事啊！”贝拉里翁道，“怎么又旧事重提？真不知你究竟几时才肯信我一回？那法子注定是要败的。”

===Original===
“Not if conducted as I would have it.” He came forward to the table, swaying from the hips in his swaggering walk. He put his finger on the map that was spread there. “If a false attack were made here, on the east, between the city and the river, so as to draw the besieged, a bold, simultaneous attack on the west might carry the walls.”

“It might,” said Bellarion slowly, and fell to considering. “This is a new thought of yours, this false attack. It has its merits.”

“You approve me for once! What condescension!”

Bellarion ignored the interruption. “It also has its dangers. The party making the feint﻿—and it will need to be a strong one or its real purpose will be guessed﻿—might easily be thrust into the river by a determined sally.”

“It will not come to that,” Carmagnola answered quickly.

“You cannot say so much.”

“Why not? The feint will draw the besieged in that direction, but before they can sally they will be recalled by the real attack striking on the other side.”

===Chinese===
“照我的法子去打就不会。”他扭动着腰胯，迈着不可一世的步子走到桌前，伸出手指点在摊开的地图上，“若在这里——城东面、城墙与河水之间——发动一次佯攻，把守军吸引过去，同时在西面胆大心细地全力猛攻，定能一举登上城头。”

“倒也有几分道理，”贝拉里翁缓缓说道，随即沉吟起来，“这佯攻的法子倒是你的新点子，确有可取之处。”

“难得你肯赞许我一回！真是屈尊降贵了！”

贝拉里翁懒得理会他的冷嘲热讽。“但这法子也藏着凶险。负责佯攻的那一路——兵力还非得够厚实不可，否则一眼便会被人看破虚实——极容易被敌军果断出城反击，一举赶进河里去。”

“绝不会闹到那步田地。”卡尔马尼奥拉急忙辩道。

“这话说得太满。”

“怎会太满？佯攻自会把守军调往东头，可等他们还没来得及出城反扑，西面主攻一响，他们立刻就得回援。”

===Original===
Bellarion pondered again; but finally shook his head.

“I have said that it has its merits, and it tempts me. But I will not take the risk.”

“The risk of what?” Carmagnola was being exasperated by that quiet, determined opposition. “God’s death! Take charge of the feint yourself, if you wish. I’ll lead the storming party, and so that you do your part, I’ll answer for it that I am inside the town before daybreak and that Theodore will be in my hands.”

Valeria had remained with her shoulders to them facing the fire. Bellarion’s entrance, discovering her in Carmagnola’s arms, had covered her with confusion, filled her with a vexation not only against himself but against Carmagnola also. From this there was no recovery until Camagnola’s words came now to promise a conclusion of their troubles far speedier than any she had dared to hope.

“You’ll answer for it?” said Bellarion. “And if you fail?”

“I will not fail. You say yourself that it is soundly planned.”

===Chinese===
贝拉里翁再次沉思片刻，末了还是摇了摇头。

“我方才说了，此计确有可取之处，连我也有些心动。可这险，我不冒。”

“冒什么险？”贝拉里翁那副不急不躁却寸步不让的阻拦，把卡尔马尼奥拉彻底激怒了，“天杀的！你若愿意，佯攻那一路你自个儿去带！主攻突击队由我亲自率领，只要你把你那一头撑住，我拿脑袋担保，天亮前必破城而入，把西奥多活捉到手里！”

瓦莱里娅一直背对着他俩站在炉火前。方才贝拉里翁推门撞见她偎在卡尔马尼奥拉怀里，教她窘迫万分，心里既恼贝拉里翁，也怪卡尔马尼奥拉。她原本一时半会儿缓不过神来，直到此刻听见卡尔马尼奥拉这番话，许诺比她敢于奢望的任何时候都要快得多地了结这桩烦难，她这才振作起来。

“你拿脑袋担保？”贝拉里翁道，“万一败了呢？”

“我不会败。你自己不也说过这计策谋划得稳妥么。”

===Original===
“Did I say so much? Surely not. To be frank, I am more afraid of Theodore of Montferrat than of any captain I’ve yet opposed.”

“Afraid!” said Carmagnola, and sneered.

“Afraid,” Bellarion repeated quietly. “I don’t charge like a bull. I like to know exactly where I am going.”

“In this case, I have told you.”

Valeria slowly crossed to them. “Make the endeavour, at least, Lord Prince,” she begged him.

He looked from one to the other of them. “Between you, you distract me a little. And you do not learn, which is really sad. Well, have your way, Francesco. The adventure may succeed. But if it fails, do not again attempt to persuade me to any course through which I do not clearly see my way.”

Valeria in her thanks was nearer to friendliness than he had ever known since that last night at Casale. Those thanks he received with a certain chill austerity.

===Chinese===
“我有说过这话？断然没有。坦白讲，比起我迄今交过手的任何将领，我最忌惮的便是蒙费拉托的西奥多。”

“忌惮！”卡尔马尼奥拉嗤笑了一声。

“正是忌惮，”贝拉里翁平静地重复道，“我打仗不像蛮牛般只顾低头猛冲。我向来喜欢把脚下的路看得清清楚楚。”

“这一回，路我已经指给你看了。”

瓦莱里娅缓缓走近二人。“亲王殿下，至少试上一回吧。”她恳求道。

他目光在二人脸上来回扫过。“你们俩一唱一和，倒教我有些心烦意乱。而且你们总是不长记性，实在叫人叹息。罢了，弗朗切斯科，依你便是。这趟冒险兴许能成。但若败了，往后凡是我看不透前路的计策，休想再劝我点头。”

瓦莱里娅连声道谢，语气之亲近，竟是自卡萨莱那一夜别后他从未见过的。面对她的谢意，他却只是冷峻而淡漠地受了。

===Original===
It was to be Carmagnola’s enterprise, and he left it to Carmagnola to make all the dispositions. The attempt was planned for the following night. It was to take place precisely at midnight, which at that time of year was the seventh hour, and the signal for launching the false attack was to be taken from the clock on San Vittore, one of the few clocks in Italy at that date to strike the hour. After an interval sufficient to allow the defenders to engage on that side, Carmagnola would open the real attack.

Empanoplied in his armour, and carrying his peaked helm in the crook of his arm, Carmagnola went to ask of the Princess a blessing on his enterprise. She broke into expressions of gratitude.

“Do not thank me yet,” he said. “Before morning, God helping me, I shall lay the State of Montferrat at your feet. Then I shall ask your thanks.”

She flushed under his ardent gaze. “I shall pray for you,” she promised him very fervently, and laid a hand upon his steel brassard. He bore it to his lips, bowed stiffly, and clanked out of the room.

===Chinese===
既说是卡尔马尼奥拉担纲的行动，贝拉里翁便将一切调度部署尽数交由他处置。奇袭定于次夜子时整发动——按那时的时令便是第七更——佯攻的号令以圣维托雷教堂（San Vittore）的钟声为准，那是当时全意大利寥寥几座能整点报时的自鸣钟之一。待隔出足够让守军被牵制在东面的工夫，卡尔马尼奥拉便发动真正的主攻。

卡尔马尼奥拉披挂得盔明甲亮，臂弯里挽着尖顶头盔，特地去向公主讨一句祝祷。她开口便是满腔感激之词。

“先别急着谢我，”他说，“蒙天主保佑，天亮之前，我必将蒙费拉托全境捧到你脚下。到那时，我再向你讨这声谢。”

在他炽热的目光注视下，她双颊泛起红晕。“我会为你祈祷的。”她满怀热忱地许诺道，并将一只手轻轻搭在他钢铁护臂上。他执起她的手凑到唇边一吻，僵直地鞠了一躬，随即甲叶铿锵地大步出了门。

===Original===
Bellarion did not come to seek her. Lightly armed, with no more than back and breast and a steel cap on his head, he led out his men through the night, making a wide détour so that their movements should not be heard in Vercelli. Since mobility was of the first importance, he took with him only a body of some eight hundred horse. They filed along by the river to the east of the city, which loomed there a vast black shadow against the faintly irradiated sky. They took up their station, dismounted, unlimbered the scaling ladders which they had brought for the purposes of their demonstration, and waited.

They were, as Bellarion calculated, close upon the appointed hour when at one point of the line there was a sudden commotion. A man had been caught who had come prowling forward, and who, upon being seized, demanded to be taken at once before their leader.

Roughly they did as he required of them. And there in the dark, for they dared kindle no betraying light, Bellarion learnt that he was a loyal subject of the Duke of Milan who had slipped out of the city to inform them that the Marquis Theodore was advised of their attack and ready to meet it.

===Chinese===
贝拉里翁却不曾来见她。他只穿了轻便的胸背护甲，头戴一顶铁盔，率领人马趁夜出发，特意绕了一个大圈，免得行军声响惊动韦尔切利城头。因机动作战全仗轻快，他只带了约八百名骑兵。大军沿着城东河岸鱼贯潜行，前方城池在微亮的天幕映衬下，矗立成一团庞大漆黑的阴影。众人抵达指定位置后下马，卸下专为佯攻造势准备的云梯，静候号令。

依贝拉里翁推算，眼看已临近约定时刻，队伍一侧忽然起了一阵骚动。哨兵抓获了一个摸黑潜行过来的人，那人被擒后，开口便要求立刻去见主帅。

兵卒们粗暴地将他押到贝拉里翁面前。因不敢点火露了行迹，二人就在漆黑中交谈。贝拉里翁这才得知，来人是米兰公爵的忠良臣民，趁夜溜出城来报信：西奥多侯爵早已得悉他们今夜要攻城，且已布下天罗地网严阵以待。

===Original===
Bellarion swore profusely, a rare thing in him who seldom allowed himself to be mastered by his temper. But his fear of Theodore’s craft drove him now like a fiery spur. If Theodore was forewarned, who could say what countermeasures Theodore had not prepared? This came of lending ear to that bellowing calf Carmagnola!

Fiercely he gave the order to mount. There was some delay in the dark, and whilst they were still being marshalled the bell of San Vittore tolled the seventh hour. Some moments after that were lost before they were spurring off to warn and withdraw Carmagnola. Even then it was necessary to go cautiously through the dark over ground now sodden by several days of rain.

Before they were halfway round the din of combat burst upon the air.

Theodore had permitted Carmagnola’s men to reach and faggot the moat, and even to plant some ladders, before moving. Then he had thrown out his army, in two wings, one from the gate to the north, the other from a gate on the opposite side, and these two wings had swept round to charge Carmagnola in flank and to envelop him.

===Chinese===
贝拉里翁破口大骂起来——他素来极少任由怒火主宰自己，此番实属罕见。实在是对西奥多老辣心机的忌惮，此刻犹如火烫的马刺般狠狠扎着他。既然西奥多早有防备，鬼晓得他又暗中备下了什么反制毒计！全怪自己一时耳根软，竟听了卡尔马尼奥拉那头蠢牛犊子瞎嚷嚷！

他厉声下令上马。黑灯瞎火里整队难免耽搁片刻，人马尚未完全列齐，圣维托雷教堂的大钟已敲响了第七更。此后又耽误了一点工夫，一行人才纵马疾驰，赶去向卡尔马尼奥拉示警并接应撤退。即便火急火燎，黑夜里在连日阴雨泡得泥泞不堪的地面上驰骋，也仍不得不小心翼翼。

他们尚未绕到半路，夜空中已骤然炸响震天动地的厮杀声。

西奥多故意放任卡尔马尼奥拉的兵马抵近护城河、抛填柴捆，甚至任由他们竖起几架云梯，这才骤然发兵。敌军分作两翼倾巢而出，一路杀出北门，另一路自南面城门涌出，两翼呈包抄之势横扫过来，从侧翼狠狠撞向卡尔马尼奥拉，企图将他围歼。

===Original===
Two things only saved Carmagnola: in the first place, Theodore’s counterattack was prematurely launched, before Carmagnola was sufficiently committed; in the second, Stoffel, taking matters into his own hands, and employing the infantry tactics advocated by Bellarion, drew off his men, and formed them up to receive the charge he heard advancing from the north. That charge cost Theodore a score of piked horses, and it failed to break through the bristling human wall that rose before it in the dark. Having flung the charge back, Stoffel, formed his men quickly into the hedgehog, embracing within it all that he could compass of Carmagnola’s other detachments, and in this formation proceeded to draw off, intent upon saving all that he could from the disaster that was upon them.

Meanwhile the other battle, issuing from the gate on the south and led by Theodore himself, had crashed into Carmagnola’s own body, which Carmagnola and Belluno were vainly seeking to marshal. They might have made an end of that detachment, which comprised the best part of Bellarion’s condotta, had not Bellarion with his eight hundred horse at last come up to charge the enemy rear. That was the saving stroke. Caught now between two masses, realising that his counter-surprise had failed, and unable in the dark to attempt a fresh manoeuvre, Theodore ordered his trumpeters to sound the retreat.

Each side accounted itself fortunate in being able to retire in good order.

## X The Arrest / 第十章 逮捕

===Original===
In the armoury of the castle of Quinto, Carmagnola paced like a caged panther, the half of his armour still hanging upon him, his blond head still encased in the close-fitting cap of bloodred velvet that served to protect it from the helmet. And as he paced, he ranted of treachery and other things to Valeria and Gian Giacomo of Montferrat, to the half-dozen captains who had returned to render with him the account of that galling failure.

The Princess occupied the big chair by the table, whilst her brother leaned upon the back of it. Beyond stood ranged Ugolino da Tenda, Ercole Belluno, Stoffel, and three others, their armour flashing in the golden light of the cluster of candles set upon the table. Over by the hearth in another high-backed chair sat Bellarion, still in his black corselet, his long legs in their mud-splashed boots stretched straight before him, his head cased in a close-fitting cap of peach-coloured velvet, disdainfully listening to Carmagnola’s furious tirade. He guessed the bitterness in the soul of the boaster who had promised so much to achieve so little. Therefore he was patient with him for a while. But to all things there must be an end, and an end there was to Bellarion’s patience.

“Talking mends nothing, Francesco,” he broke in at last.

“It may prevent a repetition.”

“There can be no repetition, because there will be no second attempt. I should never have permitted this but that you plagued me with your insistence.”

“And I should have succeeded had you done your part!” roared Carmagnola in fury, a vain, humiliated man reckless of where he cast the blame for his own failure. “By God’s Life, that is why disaster overtook us. Had you delivered your own attack as was concerted between us, Theodore must have sent a force to meet it.”

===Chinese===
在昆托城堡的军械厅里，卡尔马尼奥拉正像一头关在笼中的黑豹般来回踱步。他身上还挂着半副甲胄，那颗金发头颅仍裹在贴合头部的血红色天鹅绒软帽里——这顶软帽原是用来护住头部、免受头盔磨伤的。他一面大步走动，一面朝着蒙费拉托的瓦莱里娅与吉安·贾科莫，以及随他一同回来汇报那场奇耻大辱般惨败的六位将领，大声咆哮着叛徒卖主之类的种种罪状。

瓦莱里娅公主坐在桌旁的大扶手椅上，她弟弟则倚在椅背上。再往外站成一排的，是乌戈利诺·达·滕达、埃尔科莱·贝卢诺、斯托费尔以及另外三位将领，他们身上的铠甲在桌上那一簇蜡烛的金光照耀下寒光闪烁。在壁炉旁另一张高背椅里坐着贝拉里翁，他依然穿着那副黑色胸甲，一双套着溅满泥点的长靴的长腿笔直向前伸着，头上戴着一顶贴合头部的桃色天鹅绒软帽，满怀轻蔑地听着卡尔马尼奥拉那通狂怒的连珠炮。他猜得出这个夸下海口却一事无成的大话精心里有多苦涩，因此起初还耐着性子容他发泄一阵。但凡事总有个限度，贝拉里翁的耐心也终于到了尽头。

“光说废话于事无补，弗朗切斯科，”他终于插嘴道。

“至少能防着下回重蹈覆辙。”

“不会有重蹈覆辙的机会了，因为绝不会再有第二次尝试。若非你死缠烂打地纠缠不休，我压根儿就不会准许这场行动。”

“要是你尽到了自己那份本分，我早就成功了！”卡尔马尼奥拉狂怒地咆哮起来，这个虚荣受挫的男人早就不顾一切，只想把自家失败的罪责往外乱泼，“天主圣命在上，我们正是因此才遭此惨败！倘若你照着你我事先商定的方案发起进攻，西奥多势必得调兵去迎击你。”

===Original===
Bellarion remained calm under the accusation, and under the eyes of that company, all reproachful save Stoffel’s. The Swiss, unable to contain himself, laughed aloud.

“If the Lord Bellarion had done that, sir, you might not now be alive. It was his change of plan, and the charge he delivered upon Theodore’s rear, that enabled us to extricate ourselves, and so averted a disaster that might have been complete.”

“And whilst you are noticing that fact,” said Bellarion, “it may also be worthy of your attention that if Stoffel had not ranged his foot to receive the charge from Theodore’s right wing, and afterwards formed a hedgehog to encircle and defend you, you would not now be ranting here. It occurs to me that an expression of gratitude and praise for Stoffel would be not so much gracious as proper.”

Carmagnola glared. “Ah, yes! You support each other! We are to thank you now for a failure, which your own action helped to bring about, Bellarion.”

Bellarion continued unruffled. “The accusation impugns only your own intelligence.”

===Chinese===
面对这番指责，以及在场众人——除了斯托费尔之外——投来的满含责难的目光，贝拉里翁依旧神色泰然。那位瑞士将领却按捺不住，朗声大笑起来。

“阁下，要是贝拉里翁大人真那么干了，您这会儿只怕已经没命了。正是他临时变阵，率军猛击西奥多的后翼，才让我们得以脱身，从而避免了一场全军覆没的灭顶之灾。”

“既然你注意到了这一节，”贝拉里翁接过话头说道，“那恐怕也值得一并留意：若不是斯托费尔迅速列起步兵方阵，硬生生顶住西奥多右翼的冲锋，随后又结成刺猬阵将你们团团护在当中，你此刻也就没法站在这里高谈阔论了。依我看，对斯托费尔表达几句感激与赞许，倒算不上什么宽宏礼让，不过是分所应当罢了。”

卡尔马尼奥拉怒目而视：“啊，好啊！你们俩真是互相吹捧！这么说，一场由你自己的行径一手促成的败仗，我们如今倒还得反过来谢谢你了，贝拉里翁。”

贝拉里翁依旧从容不迫：“这种指控，不过是在怀疑你自己的智商罢了。”

===Original===
“Does it so? Does it so? Ha! Where is this man who came, you say, to tell you that Theodore was forewarned of the attack?”

Bellarion shrugged. “Do I know where he is? Do I care? Does it matter?”

“A man comes to you out of the night with such a message as that, and you don’t know what has become of him!”

“I had other things to do than think of him. I had to think of you, and get you out of the trap that threatened you.”

“And I say that you would have best done that by attacking on your own side, as we agreed.”

===Chinese===
“是吗？真是如此吗？哈！你嘴里那个半夜跑来向你报信、说西奥多早已对夜袭有所防备的人，如今上哪儿去了？”

贝拉里翁耸了耸肩：“我哪儿知道他在哪儿？我又何必管他在哪儿？这打紧吗？”

“半夜三更从黑影里钻出一个人来向你报这等要紧消息，你竟连他如今下落如何都不知道！”

“我那时还有比惦记他更要紧的事要做。我得替你着想，得把你从眼看就要合拢的罗网里拽出来。”

“而我偏要说，照原定计划从你那一侧发起进攻，才是救我的最好法子。”

===Original===
“We never agreed that I should attack. But only that I should pretend to attack. I had not the means to push home an escalade.” His suavity suddenly departed. “But it seems to me that I begin to defend myself.” He reached for his steel cap, and stood up.

“It becomes necessary!” cried Carmagnola, who in two strides was at his side.

“Only that I should defend myself from a charge of rashness in having yielded to your insistence to attempt this night-attack. There was a chance, I thought, of success, and since the alternative of starving the place would entail a delay of months, I took that chance. It has missed, and so forces me to a course I’ve been considering from the outset. Tomorrow I shall raise the siege.”

“You’ll raise the siege!”

That ejaculation of amazement came in chorus.

===Chinese===
“我们从未约定过由我主攻，约定的只是我佯装进攻。我手里本就没有能强行登城破垒的器械与兵力。”他话音里的温文尔雅骤然收敛，“不过眼下看来，我倒像是开始为自己辩解了。”他伸手抓起自己的铁盔，站起身来。

“你本就该辩解！”卡尔马尼奥拉大叫一声，两步便跨到了他身侧。

“我唯一需要辩解的，是当初不该一时轻率，竟顺了你的执意恳求，答应尝试这场夜袭。那时我寻思着兴许有几分胜算，况且若是改用困饿之计，势必得拖延数月之久，所以我才冒险一搏。既然这一搏落了空，便只能迫使我采取打一开始起就已在斟酌的方略。明天，我将下令撤围。”

“你要撤围！”

这一声惊呼几乎是众人异口同声叫出来的。

===Original===
“Not only of Vercelli, but also of Mortara.”

“You’ll raise the siege, sir?” It was Gian Giacomo who spoke now. “And what then?”

“That shall be decided tomorrow in council. It is almost daybreak. I’ll wish you a good repose, madonna, and you, sirs.” He bowed to the company and moved to the door.

Carmagnola put himself in his way. “Ah, but wait, Bellarion﻿ ﻿…”

“Tomorrow,” Bellarion’s voice was hard and peremptory. “By then your wits may be cooler and clearer. If you will all gather here at noon, you shall learn my plans. Good night.” And he went out.

===Chinese===
“不仅撤去韦尔切利之围，也一并撤去莫尔塔拉之围。”

“您要撤围，阁下？”这回开口的是吉安·贾科莫，“那之后呢？”

“这要留待明日军事会议上再作定夺。天快亮了。祝您安寝，小姐，也祝各位大人好梦。”他向众人欠身行了一礼，转身朝门口走去。

卡尔马尼奥拉跨步挡在他身前：“啊，且慢，贝拉里翁……”

“明天再说。”贝拉里翁的声音冷硬而不容置喙，“到那时，你的头脑兴许能冷静清醒些。请诸位正午时分齐聚于此，届时自会知晓我的打算。晚安。”说罢，他径自走了出去。

===Original===
They gathered there, not at noon on the morrow, but an hour before that time, summoned by messages from Carmagnola, who was the last to arrive and a prey to great excitement. Belluno, da Tenda, Stoffel, and three other officers awaited him with the Princess and the Marquis Gian Giacomo. Bellarion was not present. He had not been informed of the gathering, for reasons which Carmagnola’s first words made clear to all.

When Bellarion did arrive, punctually at noon, for the council to which he had bidden the captains, he was surprised to find them already seated about the table in debate and conducting this with a vehemence which argued that matters had already gone some way. Their voices raised in altercation reached him as he mounted the short flight of stone steps, at the foot of which a half-dozen men of Belluno’s company were lounging.

A silence fell when he entered, and all eyes at once were turned upon him. He smiled a greeting, and closed the door. But as he advanced, he began to realise that the sudden silence was unnatural and ominous.

He came to the foot of the table, where there was a vacant place. He looked at the faces on either side of it, and lastly at Carmagnola seated at its head, between Valeria and Gian Giacomo.

===Chinese===
次日他们齐聚厅中，却不是在正午，而是在那之前一个时辰——众人皆是奉卡尔马尼奥拉的传信而来的，而他自己却最后一个到场，神情间难掩极度的亢奋与激动。贝卢诺、达·滕达、斯托费尔以及另外三名军官，正陪着公主与吉安·贾科莫侯爵在厅中候着他。唯独不见贝拉里翁。这场聚会压根儿就没通知他，至于缘由，卡尔马尼奥拉一开口便教众人豁然明白了。

及至正午时分，贝拉里翁准时前来赴那场他自己约定的军事会议时，却惊讶地发现众将早已围坐在长桌旁争论不休，且言辞激烈，足见事情早已议过一阵了。他沿着那段短短的石阶往上走时——石阶脚下还懒散地站着五六个贝卢诺麾下的兵士——厅内争吵的高声便已传进了他的耳中。

他推门而入，厅内骤然一片死寂，所有目光登时齐刷刷投向了他。他微笑着点头致意，顺手掩上房门。然而待他迈步走近，便渐渐察觉到这突如其来的沉默显得极不寻常，透着几分不祥之气。

他走到长桌下首那处空位前，扫视着桌旁两侧一张张面孔，最后将目光落在了坐在上首、居于瓦莱里娅与吉安·贾科莫之间的卡尔马尼奥拉脸上。

===Original===
“What do you debate here?” he asked them.

Carmagnola answered him. His voice was hard and hostile; his blue eyes avoided the steady glance of Bellarion’s.

“We were about to send for you. We have discovered the traitor who is communicating with Theodore of Montferrat, forewarning him of our every measure, culminating in last night’s business.”

“That is something, although it comes at a time when it can no longer greatly matter. Who is your traitor?”

None answered him for a long moment. Saving Stoffel, who was flushed and smiling disdainfully, and the Princess whose eyes were lowered, they continued to stare at him and he began to mislike their stare. At last, Carmagnola pushed towards him a folded square of parchment bearing a broken seal.

“Read that.”

===Chinese===
“诸位在这里争论什么呢？”他问道。

开口回答他的是卡尔马尼奥拉。他的声音僵硬而充满敌意，一双蓝眼睛却躲闪着，不敢直视贝拉里翁沉稳镇定的目光。

“我们正要派人去请你呢。我们已经查出那个与蒙费拉托的西奥多暗通款曲、把我方一举一动乃至昨夜的行动全数提前走漏给敌人的叛徒了。”

“这倒是个收获，虽说查出来的时机未免晚了些，眼下已无甚大碍了。你们抓到的那个叛徒是谁？”

好一阵子，竟无一人应声。除了涨红了脸、嘴角挂着轻蔑冷笑的斯托费尔，以及低垂着眼帘的公主之外，其余众人皆一动不动地直盯着他看，那眼神直教他生出一股厌恶与警觉。终于，卡尔马尼奥拉将一张折成四方形、上面火漆印已然破损的羊皮纸推到了他面前。

“念念这个吧。”

===Original===
Bellarion took it, and turned it over. To his surprise he found it superscribed “To the Magnificent Lord Bellarion Cane, Prince of Valsassina.” He frowned, and a little colour kindled in his cheeks. He threw up his head, stern-eyed. “How?” he asked. “Who breaks the seals of a letter addressed to me?”

“Read the letter,” said Carmagnola, peremptorily.

Bellarion read:

> **Dear Lord and Friend**, your fidelity to me and my concerns saved Vercelli last night from a blow that in its consequences might have led to our surrender, for without your forewarning we should assuredly have been taken by surprise. I desire you to know my recognition of my debt, and to assure you again of the highest reward that it lies in my power to bestow if you continue to serve me with the same loyal devotion.
> Theodore Paleologo of Montferrat

===Chinese===
贝拉里翁拿起来翻看了一眼，不由得大为吃惊——只见封皮上赫然题写着：“致尊贵的瓦尔萨西纳亲王贝拉里翁·卡内大人”。他眉头一蹙，双颊微微泛起一丝血色。他猛地抬起头，眼神凛冽：“怎么回事？是谁擅自拆开了写给我的信笺火漆？”

“先看信。”卡尔马尼奥拉态度蛮横地说道。

贝拉里翁展开读道：

> **敬爱的大人暨挚友**：承蒙阁下对我及我方事务竭诚效忠，昨夜方能保全韦尔切利免遭一记足以迫使我军投降的重创；若无阁下事先示警，我等昨夜必遭奇袭无疑。特此致书，以明感念深恩之心，并再次向阁下保证：只要阁下继续秉此赤诚忠贞为我效力，凡我力所能及之至高赏赐，必当悉数奉上。
> 蒙费拉托的西奥多·帕莱奥洛戈

===Original===
Bellarion looked up from the letter with some anger in his face, but infinitely more contempt and even a shade of amusement.

“Where was this thing manufactured?” he asked.

Carmagnola’s answer was prompt. “In Vercelli, by the Marquis Theodore. It is in his own hand, as madonna here has testified, and it is sealed with his own seal. Do you wonder that I broke it?”

Sheer amazement overspread Bellarion’s face. He looked at the Princess, who fleetingly looked up to answer the question in his glance. “The hand is my uncle’s, sir.”

He turned the parchment over, and conned the seal with its stag device. Then the amazement passed out of his face, light broke on it, and he uttered a laugh. He turned, pulled up a stool, and sat down at the table’s foot, whence he had them all under his eye.

===Chinese===
贝拉里翁从信纸上抬起头来，脸上虽带着几分怒意，却更多是无尽的轻蔑，甚至还掺杂着一缕觉得荒唐可笑的神气。

“这玩意儿是在哪儿伪造出来的？”他问道。

卡尔马尼奥拉回答得干脆利落：“在韦尔切利，出自西奥多侯爵亲笔。正如这位小姐刚才作证确认的，这确系他本人手迹，上面也盖着他自己的印章。如此一来，你还怪我将它拆开么？”

纯粹的愕然瞬间漫上贝拉里翁的脸庞。他望向公主，公主飞快地抬起眼眸迎上他目光中的探询：“这笔迹确是我叔父的，阁下。”

贝拉里翁把羊皮纸翻过来看了看，仔细端详着那枚刻有雄鹿纹章的火漆印。旋即，他脸上的错愕消散殆尽，眼中豁然亮起明悟的光彩，竟嗤笑出声。他转过身，拉过一张凳子，在长桌下首坐了下来，从这个位置恰好能将众人尽收眼底。

===Original===
“Let us proceed with method. How did this letter reach you, Carmagnola?”

Carmagnola waved to Belluno, and Belluno, hostile of tone and manner, answered the question. “A clown coming from the direction of the city blundered into my section of the lines this morning. He begged to be taken to you. My men naturally brought him to me. I questioned him as to what he desired with you. He answered that he bore a message. I asked him what message he could be bearing to you from Vercelli. He refused to answer further, whereupon I threatened him, and he produced this letter. Seeing its seal, I took both the fellow and the letter to my Lord Carmagnola.”

Bellarion, himself, completed the tale. “And Carmagnola perceiving that seal took it upon himself to break it, and so discovered the contents to be what already he suspected.”

“That is what occurred.”

Bellarion, entirely at his ease, looked at them with amused contempt, and finally at Carmagnola in whose face he laughed.

“God save you, Carmagnola! I often wonder what will be the end of you.”

===Chinese===
“咱们不妨按章法把事情理一理。这封信是怎么到你手上的，卡尔马尼奥拉？”

卡尔马尼奥拉朝贝卢诺一挥手，贝卢诺便用充满敌意的语调与神态代为答道：“今早有个乡巴佬从城池方向走来，一头撞进了我防区的阵线里。他央求我手下带他去见你。我的人自然先把他押到了我面前。我盘问他找你有何勾当，他答说自己是来送信的。我追问他能从韦尔切利给你带什么信来，他死活不肯再说，于是我吓唬了他一番，他这才掏出了这封信。我一见上面的火漆印，便连人带信一道送交给了卡尔马尼奥拉大人。”

贝拉里翁自己接过话茬，把后半截故事补全了：“于是卡尔马尼奥拉认出了那枚印章，便自作主张拆开了信，果真从里头看出了他早已疑心有鬼的内容。”

“事情经过正是如此。”

贝拉里翁神态自若至极，带着几分好笑又轻蔑的神情环视众人，最后目光停在卡尔马尼奥拉脸上，当面笑出了声。

“愿天主保佑你吧，卡尔马尼奥拉！我真常常忍不住琢磨，你将来究竟会落个什么下场。”

===Original===
“I am no longer wondering what will be the end of you,” he was furiously answered, which only went to increase his amusement.

“And you others, you were equally deceived. The letter and Carmagnola’s advocacy of my falseness and treachery were not to be resisted?”

“I have not been deceived,” Stoffel protested.

“I was not classing you with those addled heads, Stoffel.”

“It will need more than abuse to clear you,” Tenda warned him angrily.

“You, too, Ugolino! And you, madonna, and even you Lord Marquis! Well, well! It may need more than abuse to clear me; but surely not more than this letter. Falsehood is in every line of it, in the superscription, in the seal itself.”

===Chinese===
“我倒是不必再琢磨你会落个什么下场了！”对方暴怒地回敬道，而这副模样反倒令贝拉里翁笑得更欢了。

“至于你们几位，竟也同样被蒙在鼓里？就凭这封信，加上卡尔马尼奥拉在一旁竭力坐实我背主叛逆的罪名，你们便深信不疑、再无半分抵御之力了么？”

“我可没有上当！”斯托费尔抗声辩白道。

“我原也没把你和这群昏了头的蠢材归为一类，斯托费尔。”

“光靠骂街可洗不清你的罪名！”滕达怒冲冲地警告他。

“连你也是如此，乌戈利诺！还有您，小姐，甚至连侯爵大人您也不例外！好啊，好得很！洗清我的罪名兴许不能光靠骂街，可光凭这封信本身，难道还不足以洗清么？从头到尾字字句句都是圈套造假——连信封上的题款、连那枚印章本身，无一不是破绽！”

===Original===
“How, sir?” the Princess asked him. “Do you insist that it is forged?”

“I have your word that it is not. But read the letter again.”

He tossed it to them. “The Marquis Theodore pays your wits a poor compliment, Carmagnola, and the sequel has justified him. Ask yourselves this: If I were, indeed, Theodore’s friend and ally, could he have taken a better way than this of putting it beyond my power to serve him further? It is plainly superscribed to me, so that there shall be no mistake as to the person for whom it is intended and it bears his full signature, so that there shall be no possible mistake on the score of whence it comes. In addition to that, he has sealed it with his arms, so that the first person into whose hands it falls shall be justified in ascertaining, as you did, what Theodore of Montferrat may have occasion to write to me.”

“It was expected that the soldiers who caught the clown would bear him straight to you,” Carmagnola countered.

“Was it? Is there no oddness in the fact that the clown should walk straight into your own men, Carmagnola, on a section of the line that does not lie directly between Vercelli and Quinto? But why waste time even on such trifles of evidence. Read the letter itself. Is there a single word in that which it was important to convey to me, or which would not have been conveyed otherwise if it had been intended for any purpose other than to bring me under this suspicion? Almost has Theodore overreached himself in his guile. Out of his intentness to destroy me, he has revealed his true aims.”

===Chinese===
“此话怎讲，阁下？”公主问他，“您仍咬定这信是伪造的吗？”

“既然有您作证，我自然相信不是伪造的。可你们不妨把这封信再读一遍。”

他把信纸随手抛回给他们：“卡尔马尼奥拉，西奥多侯爵显然对你的脑筋没抱多大指望，而如今的结果也证明他料事如神。你们自己摸着良心问问：倘若我当真是西奥多的盟友与内应，他若想叫我再也无法替他效力，世上还能找出比这更绝的招数么？信封上明明白白写着我的大名，生怕旁人认错了收信人；信尾又签着他的全名全衔，唯恐旁人弄不清这信打哪儿寄来。不仅如此，他还特地盖上自己的纹章大印，好叫头一个截获此信的人理直气壮地像你方才所做的那样拆信一探究竟，看看蒙费拉托的西奥多究竟有什么要紧事非得写信通知我不可。”

“兴许他指望抓到那个乡巴佬的士兵会直接把人送到你面前去呢。”卡尔马尼奥拉硬着头皮反驳道。

“指望这个？那那个乡巴佬偏偏一头撞进你自己的部下手里——而那一带防线根本不在韦尔切利通往昆托的直路上——这难道就不蹊跷么？罢了，何必还在这种鸡毛蒜皮的细节上耽搁工夫。你们读读信的正文吧。里头哪怕有半个字是什么非传达给我不可的机密么？若不是一心想借此把我拖进这桩通敌嫌疑里，里头哪句话不是换作别的法子才更合情理？西奥多耍弄权谋，险些就耍过了头。他太急着想置我于死地，反倒把自己的真实用心暴露无遗了。”

===Original===
“The very arguments I used with them,” said Stoffel.

Bellarion looked in amazement at his lieutenant. “And they failed?” he cried, incredulous.

“Of course they failed, you foul traitor!” Carmagnola bawled at him. “They are ingenious, but they are obvious to a man caught as you are.”

“It is not I that am caught; but you that are in danger of it, Carmagnola, in danger of being caught in the web that Theodore has spun.”

“To what end? To what end should he spin it? Answer that.”

===Chinese===
“我刚才跟他们掰扯的，一字不差正是这些道理。”斯托费尔说道。

贝拉里翁惊诧地望着自己的副将，难以置信地叫道：“竟然连这也说服不了他们？”

“那还用说！你这卑鄙的卖主逆贼！”卡尔马尼奥拉冲着他大吼，“这番说辞倒是巧舌如簧，可任谁被抓了个现行，都能编出这种显而易见的狡辩！”

“落网的不是我，而是你正处在这步田地里，卡尔马尼奥拉——你正要一头栽进西奥多亲手织就的罗网里去了。”

“为了什么？他费尽心机织这张网究竟是为了什么？你倒是答上来啊！”

===Original===
“Perhaps to set up dissensions amongst us, perhaps to remove the only one of the captains opposed to him whom he respects.”

“You’re modest, by God!” sneered Carmagnola.

“And you’re a purblind fool, Carmagnola,” cried Stoffel in heat.

“Then are we all fools,” said Belluno. “For we are all of the same mind on this.”

“Aye,” said Bellarion sadly. “You’re all of the same emptiness. That’s clear. Well, let us have in this clown and question him.”

“To what purpose?”

===Chinese===
“或许是为了在我们内部挑拨内讧，或许是为了除掉与他作对的众将之中唯一令他忌惮敬畏的那一个。”

“天主在上，你可真够谦虚的！”卡尔马尼奥拉冷笑连连。

“而你是个瞎了眼的蠢货，卡尔马尼奥拉！”斯托费尔怒气冲冲地喊道。

“照这么说，我们全都是蠢货了，”贝卢诺冷冷插嘴，“因为在这桩事上，我们大伙儿全都持同一看法。”

“不错，”贝拉里翁叹了口气，语带悲凉，“你们脑子里确实一样空空如也。这再明白不过了。行吧，把那个乡巴佬带进来，咱们当面盘问他一番。”

“审他有何用？”

===Original===
“That we may wring from him his precise instructions, since the letter does not suffice.”

“You take too much for granted. The letter suffices fully. You forget that it is not all the evidence against you.”

“What? Is there more?”

“There is your failure last night to make the false attack you undertook to make, and there is the intention you so rashly proclaimed here afterwards that you would raise the siege of Vercelli today. Why should you wish to do that if you are not Theodore’s friend, if you are not the canker-hearted traitor we now know you to be?”

“If I were to tell you, you would not understand. I should merely give you another proof that I am Theodore’s ally.”

“That is very probable,” said Carmagnola with a heavy sneer. “Fetch the guard, Ercole.”

===Chinese===
“既然这封信还不够明白，咱们好从他嘴里撬出他当初领到的确切指令。”

“你未免太自以为是了。单凭这封信便已铁证如山。你别忘了，指证你的罪证还不止这一件呢。”

“哦？莫非还有别的？”

“还有你昨夜违约未曾发起说好的佯攻，更有你事后在这里轻率扬言今日便要撤去韦尔切利之围的打算。若非你本就是西奥多的同党，若非你正是我们如今看穿的那个狼心狗肺的叛徒，你为何偏偏急着撤围？”

“即便我把缘由讲给你听，你也听不明白。我只会平白再多给你递上一条证明我是西奥多同党的罪证罢了。”

“这倒极有可能，”卡尔马尼奥拉阴沉地冷笑一声，“去叫卫兵来，埃尔科莱。”

===Original===
“What’s this!” Bellarion was on his feet even as Belluno rose, and Stoffel came up with him, laying hands on his weapons. But Ugolino da Tenda and another captain between them overpowered him, whilst the other two ranged themselves swiftly on Bellarion’s either hand. Bellarion looked at them, and from them again to Carmagnola. He was lost in amazement.

“Are you daring to place me under arrest?”

“Until we deliberate what shall be done with you. We shall not keep you waiting long.”

“My God!” His wits worked swiftly, and he saw clearly that they might easily work their will with him. Of the four thousand men out there, only Stoffel’s eight hundred Switzers would be on his side. The others would follow the lead of their respective captains. The leaders upon whom he could have depended in this pass﻿—Koenigshofen and Giasone Trotta﻿—were away at Mortara. Perceiving at last this danger, hitherto entirely unsuspected, he turned now to the Princess.

===Chinese===
“这是作甚！”贝卢诺才刚起身，贝拉里翁已霍然站起；斯托费尔也紧跟着窜了上来，伸手按住佩剑。然而乌戈利诺·达·滕达与另一名将领合力扑上，将斯托费尔死死制住；与此同时，其余两员将领已迅疾闪身抢到贝拉里翁左右两侧，将他夹在当中。贝拉里翁看看身旁的将领，又越过他们望向卡尔马尼奥拉，脸上满是难以置信的惊愕。

“你们竟敢下令将我逮捕？”

“姑且先关押起来，等我们商议好该如何处置你。绝不会让你等太久的。”

“我的天主啊！”贝拉里翁电光石火般飞速盘算了一遍，登时看清对方完全有能力对付自己、任所欲为。外头那四千兵马里，唯有斯托费尔麾下的八百瑞士兵会站在他这一边；其余士卒皆会听命于各自的主将。在这危急关头，他原本能指望倚仗的那两位将领——柯尼希斯霍芬与贾索内·特罗塔——此刻正远在莫尔塔拉。直到这一刻，他才猛然醒悟眼前这桩先前全然未曾料及的杀身之祸，于是转过头望向了瓦莱里娅公主。

===Original===
“Madonna,” he said, “it is you whom I serve. Once before you suspected me, in the matter of Carmagnola’s bridges, and the sequel proved you wrong.”

Slowly she raised her eyes to look at him fully for the first time since he had joined that board. They were very sorrowful and her pallor was deathly.

“There are other matters, sir, besides that, which I remember. There is the death of Enzo Spigno, for one.”

He recoiled as if she had struck him. “Spigno!” he echoed, and uttered a queer little laugh. “So it is Spigno who rises from his grave for vengeance?”

“Not for vengeance, sir. For justice. There would be that if there were not the matter that Messer Carmagnola has urged to convict you.”

“To convict me! Am I then convicted without trial?”

===Chinese===
“小姐，”他开口道，“我效忠的乃是您啊。先前在卡尔马尼奥拉架桥一事上，您也曾怀疑过我，后来的事实不是证明您错怪了我么？”

她缓缓抬起眼帘——这是自他走进这间会议厅以来，她头一回正眼直视他。她眼中满是深沉的哀痛，面色苍白如死。

“除了那桩事外，阁下，我还记着别的旧账。譬如恩佐·斯皮尼奥之死，便是其中一桩。”

他如遭重击般往后一仰：“斯皮尼奥！”他低声重复着这个名字，随即发出一声古怪的短笑，“原来竟是斯皮尼奥从坟墓里爬出来索命复仇了！”

“不是为了复仇，阁下，而是为了公道。就算没有卡尔马尼奥拉先生力陈的这桩定罪铁案，单凭那一笔账，也自有公道要讨。”

“定我的罪！莫非未曾经过审讯，便已定下我的罪名了么？”

===Original===
None answered him, and in the pause that followed the men-at-arms summoned by Belluno clanked in, and at a sign from Carmagnola closed about Bellarion. There were four of them. One of the captains deprived him of his dagger, the only weapon upon him, and flung it on the table. At last Bellarion roused himself to some show of real heat.

“Oh, but this is madness! What do you intend by me?”

“That is to be deliberated. But be under no delusive hope, Bellarion.”

“You are to decide my fate? You?” From Carmagnola, he looked at the others. He had paled a little; but amazement still rode above fear.

===Chinese===
厅中无一人作答。紧接着的片刻沉寂里，贝卢诺召来的几名甲士叮当响着铁甲鱼贯而入，循着卡尔马尼奥拉的眼色一拥而上，将贝拉里翁团团围住。进来的共有四名卫兵。其中一名将领伸手缴去了他身上唯一带着的武器——一柄短剑，随手掷在长桌上。直到此刻，贝拉里翁才终于动了真怒，声色俱厉起来。

“哦，这简直是发疯了！你们到底打算拿我怎么样？”

“这自会仔细商议。不过你休存半点幻想，贝拉里翁。”

“由你们来决定我的生死？就凭你么？”他的目光从卡尔马尼奥拉身上移向其余众人。他脸色略微泛白，然而神情间的错愕依然压过了畏惧。

===Original===
Stoffel, unable longer to contain himself, turned furiously upon Carmagnola. “You rash, vainglorious fool. If Bellarion is to be tried there is none under the Duke’s magnificence before whom he may be arraigned.”

“He has been arraigned already before us here. His guilt is clear, and he has said nothing to dispel a single hair of it. There remains only to decide his sentence.”

“This is no proper arraignment. There has been no trial, nor have you power to hold one,” Stoffel insisted.

“You are wrong, captain. There are military laws﻿ ﻿…”

“I say this is no trial. If Bellarion is to be tried, you’ll send him before the Duke.”

“And at the same time,” put in Bellarion, “you’ll send your single witness; this clown who brought that letter. Your refusal to produce him here before me now in itself shows the malice by which you’re moved.”

===Chinese===
斯托费尔再也按捺不住，猛地转向卡尔马尼奥拉怒骂起来：“你这轻率狂妄、好大喜功的蠢货！即便要审判贝拉里翁，除了尊贵的公爵殿下亲自审断，普天之下又有谁够资格对他提审定罪？”

“他方才在这里就已经受过我们的公审了。他的罪行铁证如山，而他自己却半根毫毛的嫌疑也没能洗脱。眼下剩下的，不过是定夺如何行刑罢了。”

“这算什么狗屁公审！根本未曾审讯，你们也压根儿没有权柄私设公堂！”斯托费尔硬顶了回去。

“那你就错了，队长。军中自有军法……”

“我说这根本不算审讯！真要审贝拉里翁，你们就该把他押送去见公爵！”

“同时，”贝拉里翁不紧不慢地插嘴道，“你们也别忘了把你们唯一的人证——就是那个送信来的乡巴佬——一并押过去。你们此刻百般推托，不敢把他带到我面前当庭对质，这本身就已经暴露了你们心怀歹意、蓄意构陷！”

===Original===
Carmagnola flushed under that charge, and scowlingly considered the prisoner. “If the form of trial you’ve received does not content you, and since you charge me with personal feeling, there is another I am ready to afford.” He drew himself up, and flung back his handsome head. “Trial by battle, Lord Prince.”

Over Bellarion’s white face a sneer was spread.

“And what shall it prove if you ride me down? Shall it prove more than that you have the heavier weight of brawn, that you are more practised in the lists and have the stronger thews? Does it need trial by battle to prove that?”

“God will defend the right,” said Carmagnola.

“Will he so?” Bellarion laughed. “I am glad to have your word for it. But you forget that the right to challenge lies with me, the accused. In your blundering stupidity you overlook essentials always. Your very dullness acquits you of hypocrisy. Shall I exercise that right upon the person in whose service I am carrying arms, upon the body of the Marquis Gian Giacomo of Montferrat?”

===Chinese===
被他当众拆穿，卡尔马尼奥拉脸上顿时一阵涨红，阴沉着脸怒视阶下囚，冷冷道：“既然刚才这番审断不合你的心意，你又诬称我挟嫌报复，那我倒还备着另一种审法，随时乐意奉陪。”他挺直腰板，高高扬起那颗俊朗的头颅，“那就按规矩来一场决斗裁决吧，亲王阁下。”

贝拉里翁惨白的脸上缓缓浮起一抹讥诮的冷笑。

“哪怕你策马冲锋把我撞翻在地，又能证明得了什么？难道除了证明你这身块头更沉、在比武场上练得更熟、筋骨气力比我更壮实之外，还能证明半点别的么？就为证明这些，难道还劳驾来上一场决斗裁决？”

“天主自会庇佑公理正义的一方。”卡尔马尼奥拉大言不惭地说。

“当真如此么？”贝拉里翁放声大笑，“有你这句话作保，我可真是欣慰极了。不过你怕是忘了，提出决斗挑战的权利，握在我这个被告手里。你总是这样蠢笨鲁莽，偏偏把最紧要的规矩忘在脑后。你这副实打实的糊涂劲儿，倒反而洗清了你装腔作势的嫌疑。难道你要我对着我所效命的主君——对着蒙费拉托侯爵吉安·贾科莫阁下的贵体——行使这项挑战之权么？”

===Original===
The frail boy named started, and looked up with dilating eyes. His sister cried out in very real alarm. But Carmagnola covered them with his answer.

“I am your accuser, sir: not he.”

“You are his deputy, no more,” Bellarion answered, and now the boy came to his feet, white and tense.

“He is in the right,” he announced. “I cannot refuse him.”

Smiling, Bellarion looked at Carmagnola, confused and awkward.

“Always you overreach yourself,” he mocked him. He turned to Gian Giacomo. “You could not refuse me if I asked it. But I do not ask it. I only desired to show the value of Carmagnola’s offer.”

===Chinese===
被点到名的那个体弱少年猛地一惊，睁大眼睛抬起头来。他姐姐更是发出一声真切惶急的惊呼。然而卡尔马尼奥拉急忙抢着回话，替他挡了回去。

“控告你的人是我，阁下，不是他。”

“你不过是他的副手代理罢了，别无其他身份。”贝拉里翁答道。此刻，那少年已经站起身来，脸色煞白，神情紧绷。

“他说得在理，”少年开口宣告道，“我不能拒绝他的挑战。”

贝拉里翁微笑着看向一时手足无措、尴尬难堪的卡尔马尼奥拉。

===Original===

Unanimously the captains voted for Bellarion’s death. The only dissentients were the Marquis and his sister. The latter was appalled by the swiftness with which this thing had come upon them, and shrank from being in any sense a party to the slaying of a man, however guilty. Also not only was she touched by Bellarion’s forbearance in the matter of trial by battle against her brother, but his conduct in that connection sowed in her mind the first real doubt of his guilt. Urgently she pleaded that he should be sent for trial before the Duke.
Carmagnola, in refusing, conveyed the impression of a great soul wrestling with circumstances, a noble knight placing duty above inclination. It was a part that well became his splendid person.
“Because you ask it, madonna, for one reason, because of the imputations of malice against me for another, I would give years of my life to wash my hands of him and send him to Duke Filippo Maria. But out of other considerations, in which your own and your brother’s future are concerned, I dare not. Saving perhaps Stoffel and his Swiss, the whole army demands his death. The matter has gone too far.”
The captains one and all proved him right by their own present insistence.
“Yet I do not believe him guilty,” the young Marquis startled them, “and I will be no party to the death of an innocent man.”
“Would any of us?” Carmagnola asked him. “Is there any room for doubt? The letter﻿ ﻿…”
“The letter,” the boy interrupted hotly, “is, as Bellarion says, a trick of my uncle’s to remove the one enemy he fears.”
That touched Carmagnola’s vanity with wounding effect. He dissembled the hurt. But it served to strengthen his purpose.
“That vain boaster has seduced you with his argument, eh?”
“No; not with his argument, but with his conduct. He could have challenged me to trial by combat, as he showed. What am I to stand against him? A thing of straw. Yet he declined. Was that the action of a trickster?”
“It was,” Carmagnola answered emphatically. “It was a trick to win you over. For he knew, as we all know, that a sovereign prince does not lie under that law of chivalry. He knew that if he had demanded it, you would have been within your right in appointing a deputy.”
“Why, then, did you not say so at the time?” the Princess asked him.
“Because he did not press the matter.

Are you mistaken on the death of your friend Count Spigno and what followed?”
“Ah! I was forgetting that,” she confessed.
“Remember it. And remember what he said at that table, which may, after all, be the truth. That Count Spigno has risen from the grave at last for vengeance.”

And meanwhile Belluno was seeking Bellarion in the small chamber in which they had confined him on the ground floor of the castle.
With perfect composure Bellarion heard the words of doom. He did not believe them. This sudden thing was too monstrously impossible. It was incredible the gods should have raised him so swiftly to his pinnacle of fame, merely to cast him down again for their amusement. They might make sport with him, but they would hardly carry it to the lengths of quenching his life.
His only answer now was to proffer his pinioned wrists, and beg that the cord might be cut. Belluno shook his head to that in silence. Bellarion grew indignant.
“What purpose does it serve beyond a cruelty? The window is barred; the door is strong, and there is probably a guard beyond it. I could not escape if I would.”
“You’ll be less likely to attempt it with bound wrists.”
“I’ll pass you my parole of honour to remain a prisoner.”
“You are convicted of treachery, and you know as well as I do that the parole of a convicted traitor is never taken.”
“Go to the devil, then,” said Bellarion, which so angered Belluno that he called in the guard, and ordered them to bind Bellarion’s ankles as well.
So trussed that he could move only by hops, and then at the risk of falling, they left him. He sat down on one of the two stools which with a table made up all the furniture of that bare chill place. He wagged his head and even smiled over the thought of Belluno’s refusal to accept his parole, or rather over the thought that in offering it he had no notion of keeping it.
“I’d break more than my pledged word to get out of this,” said he to himself. “And only an idiot would blame me.”
He looked round the bare stone walls, and lastly at the window. He rose, and hopped over to it. Leaning on the sill, which was at the height of his breast, he looked out.

He removed his hands, and the priest almost choked himself in his sudden greed of air.
“Why? Why do you assault me?” he gasped. “I come to comfort and﻿ ﻿…”
“I know why you come better than you do, brother. You think you bring me the promise of eternal life. All that I require from you at present is the promise of temporal existence. So we’ll leave the shriving for something more urgent.”
It would be a half-hour later, when cowled as he had entered the tall, the bowed figure of the priest emerged again from the room, bearing the lantern.
“I’ve brought the light, my son,” he said almost in a whisper. “Your prisoner desires to be alone in the dark with his thoughts.”
The man-at-arms took the lantern in one hand, whilst with the other he was driving home the bolt. Suddenly he swung the lantern to the level of the cowl. This priest did not seem quite the same as the one who had entered. The next moment, on his back, his throat gripped by the vigorous man who knelt upon him, the guard knew that his suspicions had been well-founded. Another moment and he knew nothing. For the hands that held him had hammered his head against the stone floor until consciousness was blotted out.
Bellarion extinguished the lantern, pushed the unconscious man-at-arms into the deepest shadow of that dimly lighted hall, adjusted his mantle and cowl, and went quickly out.
The soldiers in the courtyard saw in that cowled figure only the monk who had gone to shrive Bellarion. The postern was opened for him, and with a murmured “*Pax vobiscum*,” he passed out across the lesser bridge, and gained the open.

Thereafter, under cover of the night, he went at speed, the monkish gown tucked high, for he knew not how soon the sentinel he had stunned might recover to give the alarm. He was stopped by a party of men of Uri, to whom at once he made himself known, and even whilst they conducted him to their captain, the news of his presence ran like fire through the Swiss encampment.
Stoffel, who was in full armour when Bellarion entered his tent, gasped his questioning amazement whilst Bellarion threw off his mantle and white woollen habit, and stood forth in his own proper person and garments.
“We were on the point of coming for you,” Stoffel told him.
“A fool’s errand, Werner. What could you have done against three thousand men, who are ready and expecting you?” But he spoke with a warm hand firmly gripping Stoffel’s shoulders and a heart warmed, indeed, by this proof of trust and loyalty.
“Something we might have done. There was a will on our side that must be lacking on the other.”
“And the walls of Quinto? You’d have beaten your heads in vain against them, even had you succeeded in reaching them. It’s as lucky for you as for me that I’ve saved you this trouble.”
“And what now?” Stoffel asked him.
“Give the order to break camp at once. We march to Mortara to rejoin the Company of the White Dog from which I should never have separated. We’ll show Carmagnola and those Montferrine princes what Bellarion can do.”
Meanwhile they already had some notion of it. The alarm at his escape had spread through Quinto; and Carmagnola had been fetched from the lines to be informed of it in detail by a half-naked priest and a man-at-arms with a bandaged head. It had taken some time to find him. It took more for him to resolve what should be done. At last, however, he decided that Bellarion would have fled to Stoffel; so he assembled his captains, and with the whole army marched on the Swiss encampment.

But he came too late. At the last the Swiss had not waited to strike their camp, realising the danger of delay, but had departed leaving it standing.

He raged and swore, striding to and fro there in his wrath, bitterly upbraiding himself for not having taken better precautions knowing with what a trickster he had to deal, damning the priest and the sentry and the fools in the courtyard who had allowed Bellarion to walk undetected through their ranks.
She watched him, and found him less admirable than hitherto in the wildness of his ravings. Unwillingly almost her mind contrasted his behaviour under stress with the calm she had observed in Bellarion. She fetched a weary sigh. “Raging will not help you, Carmagnola,” she said at last, the least asperity in her tone.

Now you see why I meant to give him no chance.”
She kept her mind to the essence of the matter.

His overweening vanity would not permit him to admit, or even to think, so much. He laughed, confident and disdainful.

And he looked so strong and masterful, so handsome in the half-armour he still wore, a very god of war.
She held out a hand to him. “My friend, forgive my doubt. You shall be dishonoured by no more fears of mine.”
He caught her hand. He drew her out of the chair, and towards him until she brought up against his broad mailed breast. “That is the fine brave spirit that I love in you as I love all in you, Valeria. You are mine, Valeria! God made us for each other.”
“Not yet,” she said, smiling a little, her eyes downcast and veiled from his ardent glance.
“When then?” was his burning question.
“When Theodore has been whipped out of Montferrat.”
His arms tightened about her until his armour hurt her. “It is a pledge, Valeria?”
“A pledge?” she echoed on a questioning, exalted note.
“The man who does that may claim me when he wants me. I swear it.”

## XII Carmagnola’s Duty / 第十二章 卡尔马尼奥拉的职责

===Original===
My Lord of Carmagnola had shut himself up in a small room on the ground floor of the castle of Quinto to indite a letter to the High and Most Potent Duke Filippo Maria of Milan. A heavy labour this of quill on parchment for one who had little scholarship. It was a labour that fell to him so rarely that he had never perceived until now the need to equip himself with a secretary.

The Princess and her brother newly returned from Mass on that Sunday morning, four days after Bellarion’s escape, were together in the armoury discussing their situation, and differing a good deal in their views, for the mental eyes of the young Marquis were not dazzled by the effulgence of Carmagnola’s male beauty, or deceived by his histrionic attitudes.

Into their presence, almost unheralded, were ushered two men. One of these was small and slight and active as a monkey, the other a fellow of great girth with a big, red, boldly humorous face, blue eyes under black brows flanking a beak of a nose, and a sparse fringe of grey hair straggling about a gleaming bald head.

The sight of those two, who smirked and bowed, brought brother and sister very suddenly to their feet.

“Barbaresco!” she cried on a note of gladness, holding out both her hands. “And Casella!”

===Chinese===
卡尔马尼奥拉大人把自己关在昆托（Quinto）城堡底楼的一间小屋里，正提笔给至高无上、威权赫赫的米兰（Milan）公爵菲利波·玛丽亚（Filippo Maria）修书一封。于他这样一个没读过多少书的人而言，用鹅毛笔在羊皮纸上写字实在是一桩苦差事。这类差事平素极少落到他头上，以致直到此刻他才发觉，自己竟连个书记官都未曾配备。

那个星期天上午，距离贝拉里翁逃脱已过去四天。公主殿下和弟弟刚做完弥撒回来，正在军械库里商议眼下的处境，姐弟俩的看法颇有分歧——因为年轻的侯爵心明眼亮，既没有被卡尔马尼奥拉那耀眼的男子俊貌晃花，也没有被他那副装腔作势的派头蒙蔽。

几乎未及通传，便有两个人被领到了他们面前。其中一人身材矮小纤瘦，敏捷得像只猴子；另一人则体格魁梧肥硕，长着一张通红、生猛而诙谐的大脸，鹰钩鼻两侧，浓黑的眉毛下嵌着一双蓝眼睛，光亮的秃顶周围稀稀疏疏地垂着一圈灰白头发。

一见这两个人陪着笑脸鞠躬行礼，姐弟俩登时霍然起身。

“巴巴雷斯科（Barbaresco）！”她惊喜地叫出声来，伸出双手，“还有卡塞拉（Casella）！”

===Original===
“And,” said Barbaresco, as he rolled forward, “near upon another five hundred refugees from Montferrat, both Guelph and Ghibelline, whom we’ve been collecting in Piedmont and Lombardy to swell the army of the great Bellarion and settle accounts with Master Theodore.”

They kissed her hands, and then her brother’s. “My Lord Marquis!” cried the fire-eating Casella, his gimlet glance appraising the lad. “You’re so well grown I should hardly have known you. We are your servants, my lord, as madonna here can tell you. For years have we laboured for you and suffered for you. But we touch the end of all that now, as do you. Theodore is brought to bay at last. We are hounds to help you pull him down.”

At no season could their coming have been more welcome or uplifting than in this hour of dark depression, when recruits to the cause of the young Marquis were so urgently required. This she told them, announcing their arrival a good omen. Servants were summoned, and despatched for wine, and whilst the newcomers drank the hot spiced beverage provided they learnt the true meaning of her words.

It sobered their exultation. This defection of Bellarion and his powerful company amounting to more than half of the entire army altered their outlook completely.

===Chinese===
“不仅如此，”巴巴雷斯科大步流星地走上前来，说道，“还有将近五百名蒙费拉托（Montferrat）的流亡者，归尔甫派（Guelph）和吉伯林派（Ghibelline）都有，是我们一路在皮埃蒙特（Piedmont）和伦巴第（Lombardy）四处网罗来的，好壮大伟大的贝拉里翁麾下的大军，跟泰奥多罗（Theodore）老爷算算总账。”

两人吻了她的手，接着又吻了她弟弟的手。“侯爵大人！”脾气火爆的卡塞拉喊道，一双锥子似的利眼上下打量着少年，“您长这么高大了，我差点儿认不出来了。大人，我们都是您的忠仆，这位小姐可以为您作证。这么些年来，我们一直为您奔走效劳，历尽艰辛。可如今，这一切总算要苦尽甘来了，您也是如此。泰奥多罗终于走投无路了。我们就是来帮您将他扑倒撕碎的猎犬。”

在这愁云惨雾、急需为年轻侯爵招兵买马的紧要关头，他们的到来再合时宜、再振奋人心不过了。公主把这番意思告诉了他们，直说他们的出现是个好兆头。她随即唤来仆人去取酒，两个风尘仆仆的来客一面喝着送来的热香料酒，一面听她道出这番话背后的真正缘由。

这番话顿时给他们的欣喜浇了一盆冷水。贝拉里翁连同他那支占全军半数以上的精锐部队一走，眼前的局势就彻底变了样。

Barbaresco blew out his great cheeks, frowning darkly.

“You say that Bellarion is the agent of Theodore?” he cried.

“We have proof of it,” she sadly assured him, and told him of the letter. His amazement deepened. “Does it surprise you, then?” she asked. “Surely it should be no news to you!”

“Once it would not have been. For once I thought that I held proof of the same; that was on the night that Spigno died at his hands. Later, before that same night was out, I understood better why he killed Spigno.”

“You understood? Why he killed him?” She was white to the lips. Gian Giacomo was leaning forward across the table, his face eager. She uttered a fretful laugh. “He killed him because he was my friend, mine and my brother’s, the chief of all our friends.”

Barbaresco shook his great head. “He killed him because this Spigno whom we all trusted so completely was a spy of Theodore’s.”

巴巴雷斯科鼓起两腮，眉头紧锁，脸色阴沉下来。

“您说贝拉里翁是泰奥多罗的密探？”他大声问道。

“我们有确凿的证据，”她伤心地向他证实，把那封信的事告诉了他。他听罢愈发惊愕。“怎么，这让您很吃惊吗？”她问道，“您肯定早就不该觉得稀奇了呀！”

“要是在从前，我确实不会吃惊。因为我也一度以为自己手里握着同样的证据——那还是在斯皮尼奥（Spigno）死在他手里的那天夜里。可后来，还没等那一夜过去，我就明白他为什么要杀斯皮尼奥了。”

“您明白了？明白他为什么杀他？”她的嘴唇瞬间失了血色。吉安·贾科莫（Gian Giacomo）越过桌子探出身子，满脸急切。她发出了一声恼怒的冷笑。“他杀他，只因为他是我的朋友，是我和我弟弟的朋友，是我们所有朋友里最忠心的一个。”

巴巴雷斯科摇了摇他那颗大脑袋。“他杀他，是因为这个我们大家曾深信不疑的斯皮尼奥，其实是泰奥多罗安插的奸细。”

===Original===
“What?”

Her world reeled about her; her senses battled in a mist. The thick, droning voice of Barbaresco came to deepen her confusion.

“It is all so simple; so very clear. The facts that Spigno was dressed as we found him and in the attic where we had imprisoned Bellarion should in themselves have explained everything. How came he there? Bellarion was all but convicted of being an agent of Theodore’s. But for Spigno we should have dealt with him out of hand. Then at dead of night Spigno went to liberate him, and by that very act convicted himself in Bellarion’s eyes. And for that Bellarion stabbed him. The only flaw is how one agent of Theodore’s should have come to be under such a misapprehension about the other. Saving that the thing would have been clear at once.”

“That I can explain,” said Valeria breathlessly, “if you have sound proof of Spigno’s guilt, if it is not all based on rash assumption.”

“Assumption!” laughed Casella, and he took up the tale. “That night, when we determined upon flight, we first repaired, because of our suspicions, to Spigno’s lodging. We found there a letter addressed superscribed to Theodore, to be delivered in the event of Spigno’s death or disappearance. Within it we found a list of our names and of the part which each of us had had in the plot to kill the Regent, and the terms of that letter made it more than clear that throughout Spigno had been Theodore’s agent for the destruction of the Marquis here.”

“That letter,” said Barbaresco, “was a safeguard the scoundrel had prepared in the event of discovery. The threat of its despatch to Theodore would have been used to compel us to hold our hands. Oh, a subtle villain, your best and most loyal friend Count Spigno, and but for Bellarion﻿ ﻿…” He spread his hands and laughed.

===Chinese===
“什么？”

她只觉天旋地转，神思仿佛在迷雾中苦苦挣扎。巴巴雷斯科那低沉浑厚的嗡嗡嗓音继续响起，愈发搅乱了她的心绪。

“这事再简单不过，再清楚不过。单看我们发现斯皮尼奥时的那身打扮，还有他死在我们关押贝拉里翁的阁楼里这两个事实，本就足以说明一切了。他怎么会出现在那儿？当时贝拉里翁几乎已经被定罪，认定是泰奥多罗的密探了。要不是斯皮尼奥拦着，我们当场就会结果了他。接着到了半夜，斯皮尼奥又悄悄去放他走——单是这一举动，就在贝拉里翁眼里坐实了自己的罪名。贝拉里翁正是为此才一刀刺死了他。唯一的破绽，是泰奥多罗的两个密探怎么会对彼此产生这么大的误会。若非这一点，整件事早就一目了然了。”

“这一点我倒能解释，”瓦莱里娅（Valeria）屏息说道，“前提是你们手里真有斯皮尼奥通敌的铁证，而不全是草率的臆测。”

“臆测！”卡塞拉大笑一声，接过话头讲了起来，“那天夜里，我们决定逃亡之前，因为早就起了疑心，先去了一趟斯皮尼奥的住处。我们在那儿搜出一封信，信封上写着呈交泰奥多罗亲启，嘱咐万一斯皮尼奥身亡或失踪便即刻送出。信里开列了我们一干人的名单，详述了我们各自在刺杀摄政王的密谋中所起的作用；而且从那封信的措辞里可以看得一清二楚，自始至终，斯皮尼奥都是泰奥多罗派来毁掉这位侯爵大人的密探。”

“那封信，”巴巴雷斯科接口道，“是那恶棍为防事情败露而备下的保命符。他本打算一旦被我们识破，就拿把信寄给泰奥多罗相要挟，逼我们束手就范。呵，真是好一个老谋深算的奸贼，您那位最要好、最忠心的朋友斯皮尼奥伯爵！若不是贝拉里翁……”他摊开双手，大笑起来。

===Original===
Then Casella interposed.

“You said, madonna, that you could supply the link that’s missing in our chain.”

But she was not listening. She sat with drooping head, her hands listlessly folded in her lap.

“It was all true. All true!” Her tone seemed the utterance of a broken heart. “And I have mistrusted him, and﻿ ﻿… Oh, God!” she cried out. “When I think that by now he might have been strangled and with my consent. And now﻿ ﻿…”

“And now,” cut in her brother almost brutally considering the pain she was already bearing, “you and that swaggering fool Carmagnola have between you driven him out and perhaps set him against us.”

===Chinese===
这时卡塞拉插话道：

“您方才说，小姐，您能补上我们这条线索里缺的那一环。”

可她根本没有在听。她低垂着头坐在那儿，双手无力地交叠在膝上。

“全都是真的。全都是真的！”她的声音仿佛是从一颗破碎的心里吐出来的，“可我却怀疑了他，而且……哦，天哪！”她失声痛呼，“一想到他差一点就被绞死了，还是经我点头同意的……而现在……”

“而现在，”她弟弟冷酷地打断了她——全然不顾她本就承受着巨大的痛苦，“你和那个装腔作势的蠢货卡尔马尼奥拉联手把他逼走了，搞不好还把他推到了我们的对立面。”

===Original===
The swaggering fool came in at that moment with inky fingers and disordered hair. The phrase that greeted him brought him to a halt on the threshold, his attitude magnificent.

“What’s this?” he asked with immense dignity.

He was told, by Gian Giacomo, so fiercely and unsparingly that he went red and white by turns as he listened. Then, commanding himself and wrapped in his dignity as in a mantle, he came slowly forward. He even smiled, condescendingly.

“Of all this that you tell I know nothing. It may well be as you say. It is no concern of mine. What concerns me is what has happened here; the discovery that Bellarion was in correspondence with Theodore, and his avowed intention to raise this siege; add to this that he has slipped through our hands, and is now abroad to work your ruin, and consider if you are justified in using hard words to me but for whom your ruin would already have been encompassed.”

His majestic air and his display of magnanimity under their reproach imposed upon all but Valeria.

===Chinese===
那个装腔作势的蠢货恰在此时走了进来，手指上沾着墨水，头发也乱蓬蓬的。迎面撞上这么一句话，他顿时在门槛上停住脚步，摆出了一副威严无比的架势。

“这是怎么回事？”他极有派头地问道。

吉安·贾科莫把事情原委劈头盖脸地告诉了他，言语之犀利毫不留情，听得他脸上一阵红一阵白。随后，他强自镇定下来，像披上一件斗篷似的裹紧自己的尊严，缓缓步入室内。他甚至还居高临下地微笑了一下。

“你们说的这些陈年旧事，我一概不知。也许真如你们所说吧。这与我无关。我关心的是眼下这里发生的事：我们查明贝拉里翁与泰奥多罗暗中通信往来，而且他自己也公开宣称意在撤围解兵；再加上他如今已从我们手中溜走，正逍遥在外图谋置你们于死地——你们自己掂量掂量，要不是有我，你们早已大祸临头，如今竟这样对我恶语相向，到底有没有道理。”

他那副凛然不可侵犯的气度，加上受人指责时展现出的宽宏大量，把在场众人都唬住了，唯独瓦莱里娅除外。

It was she who answered him:

“You are forgetting that it was only my conviction that he had been Theodore’s agent aforetime which disposed me to believe him Theodore’s agent now.”

“But the letter, then?” Carmagnola was showing signs of exasperation.

“In God’s name, where is this letter?” growled the deep voice of Barbaresco.

===Chinese===
开口回应他的是她：

“可那封信又作何解释呢？”卡尔马尼奥拉露出了恼火的神色。

“看在上帝的份上，那封信到底在哪儿？”巴巴雷斯科低沉的嗓门吼了起来。

===Original===
“Who are you to question me now? I do not know your right, sir, or even your name.”

The Princess presented him and at the same time Casella.

Impatiently Carmagnola produced it from the scrip that hung beside his dagger from a gold-embossed girdle of crimson leather.

Slowly Barbaresco spelled it out, Casella reading over his shoulder. When he had done, he looked at Carmagnola, and from Carmagnola to the others, first in sheer amazement, then in scornful mirth.

===Chinese===
“你是什么人，竟敢这般质问我？阁下，我既不知你凭什么发问，甚至连你的名字都不知道。”

“大人，他们都是我久已敬重的老友，此番带着所能纠集的一切兵力前来为我效力。请把那封信拿给巴巴雷斯科先生瞧瞧吧。”

卡尔马尼奥拉不耐烦地从挂袋里掏出信来——那只挂袋和他的匕首一起，悬在一条缀有金饰的深红皮腰带上。

巴巴雷斯科慢条斯理地拼读着信上的字句，卡塞拉探头在他肩后一同观看。读罢，他抬眼看向卡尔马尼奥拉，又从卡尔马尼奥拉扫视到其余众人，起初满脸愕然，继而化作一阵轻蔑的哂笑。

===Original===
“Lord of Heaven, Messer Carmagnola! You’ve the repute of a great fighter, and, to be sure, you’re a fine figure of a man; also I must assume you honest. But I would sooner put my trust in your animal strength than in your wits.”

“Sir!”

“Oh, aye, to be sure, you can throw out your chest and roar and strut. But use your brains for once, man.” The boldly humorous red face was overspread by a sardonic grin. “Master Theodore took your measure shrewdly when he thought to impose upon you with this foxy piece of buffoonery, and, my faith, if Bellarion had been less nimble, this trick would have served its purpose. Nay, now don’t puff and blow and swell! Read the letter again. Ask yourself if it would have borne that full signature and that superscription if it had been sincere, and considering that it imparts no useful information save that Bellarion was betraying you, ask yourself if it would have been written at all had anything it says been true.”

“The very arguments that Bellarion used,” cried the Marquis.

“To which we would not listen,” said the Princess bitterly.

Carmagnola sniffed. “They are the arguments any man in his case would use. You overlook that the letter is an incentive, an undertaking to reward him suitably if he﻿ ﻿…”

===Chinese===
“老天爷啊，卡尔马尼奥拉先生！您素有沙场猛将之名，而且说实在的，您确实生得一表人才；我也姑且当您为人忠厚。可要说办事，我宁愿指望您那一身蛮力，也不敢指望您的脑子。”

“阁下！”

“哦，对，没错，您自然会挺起胸膛、大吼大叫、昂首阔步。可您就用一回脑子吧，好汉。”那张生猛诙谐的红脸蛋上浮现出讽刺的咧嘴大笑，“泰奥多罗老爷可把您的斤两摸得透透的，才会异想天开，想用这么个狡猾的拙劣把戏来糊弄您；说真的，要不是贝拉里翁手脚麻利，这圈套还真就得逞了。哎，别吹胡子瞪眼、喘粗气、鼓肚子啦！把这信再读一遍。您自己问问自己，这信要是当真的，上头会写得着这么全的名姓和收信人题署吗？再想想，这信里除了白纸黑字说贝拉里翁背叛了您之外，半点有用的消息也没透露——您问问自己，要是信里说的有半句真话，这信还会写出来吗？”

“而我们偏偏不肯听信，”公主苦涩地说道。

Barbaresco broke in, exasperated by the man’s grandiose stupidity.

“To the devil with that, numskull!”

“Numskull, sir? To me? By Heaven﻿ ﻿…”

“Sirs, sirs!” The Princess laid her hand on Barbaresco’s great arm. “This is not seemly to my Lord Carmagnola﻿ ﻿…”

“I know it. I know it. I crave his pardon. But I was never taught to suffer fools gladly. I﻿ ﻿…”

“Sir, your every word is an offence. You﻿ ﻿…”

===Chinese===
巴巴雷斯科被这人狂妄自大的蠢态气得忍无可忍，粗暴地打断了他。

“去你的吧，榆木脑袋！”

“榆木脑袋，阁下？您是在骂我？老天爷……”

“我知道，我知道。我向他赔罪便是。可我打小就没学会怎么心平气和地容忍蠢人。我……”
